t: a purchase is not acquired by words. By an oral agreement between the parties; an act of acquisition is required (for the exceptional case of things acquired by speech, see Hilchot Ishut 23:13).
and they fixed the price. They set the price.
it is nothing. Nevertheless, it is proper for a person to keep his word and carry out the sale (below 7:8).
and likewise with one who gives a gift and one who receives it. They must perform an act of acquisition (for the ways of acquiring a gift see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah, chapter 3).

and they do not need witnesses at all. The sale takes effect even without witnesses (see also below 5:9). Unlike betrothal and divorce, where an act has no validity at all without witnesses (Hilchot Ishut 4:6, Hilchot Gerushin 1:1).
and neither of them can retract. Regret the sale.
land is acquired in one of three ways. And see below 5:5, where it is mentioned that land is also acquired by exchange.
by taking possession. An act on the land itself (below, halakhah 8).
in a place where they do not write the deed. Where it is their custom not to be particular about this, and they are satisfied with the giving of the money.
he has not acquired until he writes the deed. Because they do not intend to complete the transaction without a deed.
for less than the value of a perutah. For in many halakhic matters such a small sum is not considered money (see, for example, Hilchot Shevu'ot 7:16, Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 3:6).
if I wish I will acquire with money, or I will acquire with a deed. I will decide whether the money or the deed completes the sale.

and he gave the money on this condition, it stands. The condition is valid both in a place where it is customary to write a deed and where it is not, for any monetary condition is valid (below 13:3 and elsewhere).

he acquired the house by the law of a guarantor. When a person tells another to lend money to a third party and that he will be guarantor for repayment of the debt, the guarantor becomes obligated to the lender even though the loan money never reached him (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 25:2). In the same way, a person can transfer property to another even if the payment for the transfer was given to a third party and not to the seller himself.

or on a leaf. And it is no problem that the deed will not last, since the deed itself effects the acquisition and is not meant as evidence of the acquisition (see also Hilchot Gerushin 4:3 regarding a get).
that the deed reached his hand. The buyer's.
even though there are no witnesses at all. There is no need for witnesses to testify to the sale, as above, halakhah 2.
in what case does this apply. That the acquisition is complete with the delivery of the deed before the seller received the money.

to one who sells his field because of its poor quality. That he sold the field because it was bad and he wanted to be rid of it, not because he needed money, and therefore he firmly decides in his mind to transfer it even before he received the payment.
provided that he improves it by his actions. That there is benefit in this for the preservation or functioning of the field, and see further below, halakhot 10-12.
if he took possession in the presence of the seller. For since he does it in his presence and with his knowledge, it is understood that he agrees that he acquire by taking possession.
his bucket. That is used for drawing water from the well.

and then opened it again. Even though he opened it again after locking, the locking is nevertheless considered an act of acquisition. It can be explained that the opening after the locking is necessary to complete the acquisition, because the opening proves that this was not an ordinary locking (for sometimes a person locks another's house as his agent), but a locking done solely for the purpose of acquisition (both explanations are cited in Kesef Mishneh).
he used it with a useful use. That the locking is effective for guarding the house as his own private house (Maggid Mishneh, below, halakhah 15).
and completed it to ten. Handbreadths.
a bundle. A group of stones.
by which he connected the water to the field. That the stones he placed channel the flow of water to the field.
by removing which he opened the water to the field. That the stones had blocked water from entering the field.
one who sells a field to his fellow adjacent to his own field. The buyer has a field next to the field he now wishes to buy.

who trampled the boundary strip between the two fields so that the two became like one field. That he walked on the raised border that was between the two fields, and trampled and flattened it until both look like one field (see below 19:2).
he acquired. Since this action constitutes an improvement of the field.
but if he walked in it. An ordinary walk, without trampling.
a vineyard path. A path that passes between vineyards and is used for passage between fields.
and what is the measure of the width of the road. When he bought a path within his fellow's field and they did not specify its width.
if it was defined by partitions. If it had defined partitions.

enough to lift one foot and place a foot beside it. Even if between the partitions there is only a narrow space sufficient just for a person to walk and not convenient for carrying a load, the buyer cannot demand more than that, since he saw that the path was defined by partitions and agreed to it.
so that it can rest on his head.

a bundle of branches, and turn around with it. The seller must give the buyer a path wide enough that one can carry a load of vine shoots on the head and turn around with the load (the explanation of the whole halakhah follows Ri Migash, Bava Batra 100a; and see Maggid Mishneh for another explanation).
a bare rock. A rock exposed, without soil or vegetation.
plowed it. Plowed it.
or gathered the fruit of the tree. See also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 2:2.
pruned it. Cut branches from the tree to improve it.
he has acquired. For these acts prove ownership of the field.
for he has revealed his intent that he transferred it to him. For had he not sold or given it, he would not assist him and give him from the field's fruit (see also Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 11:9).
and a Jew who comes by right of the gentile. Who bought land from the gentile.

he acquires only by a deed. Together with money, according to the law of the gentile (Kesef Mishneh). The reason for the law is that the Jew fears the gentile will retract, and the Jew's mind is satisfied only with an acquisition made by writing a deed together with the payment (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 1:14).
like movable property for acquisition. For the laws of purchase and sale.

and they are subject to overcharge. For with movable property, a deviation from the market price may cause the sale to be annulled or part of the money to be returned (see below 12:1-4), but land is not subject to overcharge (below 13:8).
in ten provinces. In different places.
once he took possession of one of them, he acquired all of them. Because all lands are connected to one another, for the foundation of all of them is one (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 27b).
a depression. A low place, a small valley.
for the use of this one, etc.. Even though their uses differ.

in what case does this apply, where he gave the price of all of them. For the seller does not firmly decide to sell several fields until he receives the price of all of them. And since this refers to a place where one does not acquire with money alone, an act of taking possession must also be performed (Maggid Mishneh).
if all were by gift, he acquired all of them. For the giver surely intended to transfer all of them to him when he takes possession of one of them.
once he took possession of one of them, he acquired all of them. Even if he did not give money, since rent is usually paid at the end of the period (Kesef Mishneh).
like land for acquisition. For the laws of a Canaanite slave were equated with land in many matters (see, for example, Hilchot Genevah 2:2, Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 5:1).
and he is acquired by money, by a deed, or by taking possession. And also by exchange (below 5:5; Hilchot Avadim 5:1).
in the presence of his master. In the presence of his previous owner (and see below, halakhah 3, for the law if he used him not in the presence of the master).
removed his shoe, etc.. The slave performed for the buyer one of these services.
anointed him. With oil.
scraped him. Scraped off the oil with which he had anointed him.
if the master lifted the slave he acquired him. Not by the acquisition of taking possession, but by the acquisition of lifting that acquires animals and movable property (below, halakhah 5, and 3:1).
seized him. Held him by force.
for slaves are acquired by such pulling. See also Hilchot Avadim 5:1. And such pulling is considered taking possession (Rabbi Chaim ben Shmuel, Kiddushin 22b, Even HaEzel).
but if he called the slave... he did not acquire. Because the slave goes of his own will, for he has a choice whether to come or not (based on the Babylonian Talmud there).
or he uses him in the manner we have explained. Above, halakhah 2.

and if he took possession of him not in the presence of the master, he must say to him: go take possession and acquire. For the acquisition of taking possession must be done in the presence of the owners or at their command (see above 1:8).

therefore he is acquired by pulling even though he did not seize him. Like an animal, which is acquired by pulling when it walks because it was called (below, halakhah 6; and see also Hilchot Avadim 5:1).
small livestock. Sheep and goats.
large livestock. Cattle.
even though it is possible to lift it. And generally something that can be lifted is acquired by lifting and not by pulling (see below 3:1-2).
they did not require him to lift it because it thrashes about on the ground. It grips the ground and is hard to lift (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:4).
and lifting, etc.. See also below 4:3.
and lifting acquires in any place. Even in a domain not belonging to the buyer, for lifting the object is like bringing it into the house of the one who lifts.

but pulling acquires only in a side alley. A path, a small lane that is not a place of public passage and where each person has permission to put his belongings. If he pulled an object there, it is as if he brought it into his own domain, and likewise in a courtyard shared by both. But in the public domain or in a courtyard that does not belong to both, the buyer has no permission to put his belongings there, and if he pulled, it is not considered as if he brought it into his domain.
that he struck it. Hit it.
and it ran. And it ran.
provided that he pulls in the presence of the owners, etc.. As stated above 1:8 regarding acquisition by taking possession.
for handing over this animal is like saying to him: go pull and acquire. Like the law of handing over a key or a bucket (above 1:9).
pull and you will acquire. Which is future tense, and not the wording of a command.
pull this cow. Now.
he did not acquire. The pulling he did was not effective, since it was not done at the time of the transfer.
acquire from now and after thirty days. The acquisition takes effect now, but the cow will pass into your possession in practice in thirty days.
even if it was standing in a pasture. A grazing place, which does not belong to the buyer.

for this is like transferring from now on condition, etc.. When a person transfers to his fellow on condition, when the condition is fulfilled it becomes clear that the acquisition made at the outset indeed took effect. So too in this case, the seller transferred the cow at the time of the pulling, but stipulated with the buyer that he wait thirty days.

one who says 'on condition that' is like one who says 'from now'. For example, if he said 'pull this animal on condition that you give me one hundred dinars,' it means that if he gives him the money the acquisition takes effect from the time of the pulling.
he did not acquire, because it is not the way of people to ride in the city. Because the seller insisted that the acquisition be made in the usual manner in which people use an animal.
who was a woman. Who lacks the strength to hold the animal so it does not run away, and therefore is accustomed to ride on it.
for the crowds press there. If he were to pull it there, it might slip away from him (and although pulling does not acquire in the public domain, riding acquires even there - Meiri, Bava Metzia 9a).
and provided that it walks with him. On condition that it walks because they are riding on it.
movable property. Objects and anything not attached to the ground (and not a person).
is acquired with money by Torah law. By the acquisition of money, like land and slaves (above 1:3, 2:1).
but the Sages instituted, etc.. The reason for the enactment is explained below, halakhah 5.
only by lifting or by pulling something that is not usually lifted. See below 4:3 for details of the places where these acquisitions are possible.
a large load. A large, heavy load.
to untie the bundle and lift it log by log. To undo the knot and lift each log separately.
and the like. A load of small fruits.
for one person cannot lift it. A single person is unable to lift it himself.
and it would be a great effort for him. Excessive effort to lift each fruit separately.
and it can be pulled only by many. Only many people together can pull it.
by handing over. That the buyer holds it with the seller's consent (Meiri, Bava Batra 75b; and see below 4:3 for details of the places where this acquisition is possible).
even though he gave all the money, he can retract. Even so, it is not proper to do so, and the court curses one who retracts (see below 7:1-2).
and why did the Sages institute this. That money does not acquire.
if it would be in the buyer's possession. If the object would be considered the buyer's property while still in the seller's house.
the seller would delay and not rescue it. For he has no loss if the object is damaged.
he would be liable to pay. To return the money to the buyer, as stated in the next halakhah.
for the Sages instituted pulling. And before the pulling the object belongs to the seller and the money to the buyer.

the Sages did not institute pulling for him, for the purchase is already in the buyer's possession. And the buyer acquired it automatically by the acquisition of a courtyard (see Maggid Mishneh and Even HaEzel; and see Hilchot Sechirut 6:5, that a person's courtyard acquires for him even if it is rented to another).
for they were made in his domain. Since he rented the place, he acquires the movable property standing in it by the acquisition of a courtyard (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:8-9).
and we have already explained. Above 1:18.

the movable property is acquired along with it. The movable property is considered secondary to the land, and therefore the buyer or the recipient of the gift acquires it together with the land (this acquisition is called 'acquisition by means of land').
acquire the movable property along with the land. Together with the land, by means of the land.
and any amount of land. A minimal piece of land.

the second did not acquire the movable property, and if he seized it after the transferor retracted, etc.. The Gemara (Kiddushin 27a) was in doubt whether one can transfer by means of land when transferring to two people, and did not resolve this doubt. Therefore the halakhah is as in any monetary doubt, that the movable property belongs to the seller, who is in possession of it, by the principle that 'the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow'; and if the buyer already seized the movable property, it is not taken from his hand, for he is now the one in possession (for this principle see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:11 and elsewhere).

even though he said to him... for the slave walks of his own will. When the seller says 'acquire movable property along with the land,' by the force of his statement the movable property becomes secondary to the land and is acquired with it even when it is not lying on it (as above, halakhah 9), since the seller can bring it and place it on the land. But a slave who walks of his own will - the seller cannot make him secondary to the land, and therefore only when the slave actually stands on the land is he considered secondary to it (Even HaEzel).
unless the movable property was on the slave's back. Lying on him, and since he acquired the slave, the slave becomes like his courtyard that acquires for him the objects in it.
and provided that he is bound. For a walking courtyard does not acquire, as below, halakhah 13 (see also Hilchot Gerushin 5:18).
and acquire the vessels on it. Only, but not the animal itself.
he did not acquire the vessels on it. For the animal belongs to the seller and cannot serve as the buyer's courtyard.

a perforated flowerpot. A flowerpot is a vessel containing soil in which seeds grow, and when the vessel has a hole in the bottom the plants are considered attached to the ground for many halakhic purposes (see, for example, Hilchot Terumot 5:15).
and the seeds in it belong to another. The vessel belongs to one person and the seeds to another.
once he pulled, he acquired. The pot is acquired by pulling, since it is movable property.
he did not acquire until he takes possession. That he performs work as in the law of taking possession of land, or acquires them by a deed or by money, for the seeds have the status of land.
if he took possession of the pot... the pot too he did not acquire. For movable property is not acquired by taking possession.
if he took possession of the seeds, he acquired the pot. He acquired the pot along with the seeds.
property without security. Movable property (for this property is not liable for the debts of its owner: if a person who owes money sold his movables, the creditor cannot collect from them).
property with security. Land (upon which responsibility for debts rests, and the creditor may collect from it even if it was sold to another - Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 3:7).
as we have explained. Above 1:17.
we have already explained. Above 1:17.
it is like something cut off. And not like land, because it no longer needs it.
clear the ground for me. Clear the ground of the vegetation on it.

once he pulled out any amount, he acquired everything because of this condition. For all the flax in the field is considered the payment for the pulling, as they agreed between them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 5:7, Ri Migash there 86b, and see Even HaEzel).
he transferred this flax to him by sale or by gift, etc.. Not in the manner stated, his taking hold of a little of the flax does not take effect for all of it.
any place where he may put it. Any place where he is permitted to put it, such as a domain belonging to him, or a side public place (a 'simta' - a small lane).
that were made. That were placed.

and not in the seller's domain, unless the transferor said to him: go and acquire with this vessel. For by this statement it is considered as if he had transferred the place to him (Ri Migash, Bava Batra 85b).
and likewise if he first acquired the vessel. From the same person from whom he is buying the fruit.
just as the buyer's vessel does not acquire for him in the seller's domain. For a person cannot acquire in another person's domain.
so the seller's vessel does not acquire for the buyer. For a person cannot acquire with another person's vessel.

handing over acquires only in the public domain... and pulling acquires only in a side alley, etc.. Handing over is an acquisition made by the buyer's holding the object with the seller's consent, and it applies to objects that are not usually pulled (above 3:3-4). In handing over, when the buyer holds the object it is considered as if it were in his hand, and he thereby acquires it. This acquisition acquires only in the public domain or in the courtyard of a third party, in which neither the seller nor the buyer has permission to put objects, for in these places the location of the object has no significance and the mere holding of the object by the person proves his ownership of it. But when the object is in a place where the seller has permission to put his belongings (a side alley or a courtyard of both), the place where the object lies is considered as belonging to the seller, and therefore the buyer's holding the object is not enough to remove it from the seller's hand. By contrast, pulling acquires by the buyer pulling the object from the seller's domain to a place considered his own, and it is effective in a shared courtyard and in a side alley, where both seller and buyer may place their belongings and the place where the object lies is considered as belonging to its owner; hence, when the buyer pulls the object, it is as if he removed it from the seller's domain and transferred it to his own. But in the public domain or in a courtyard of a third party, pulling from place to place has no significance, since he cannot pull the object to a place considered his domain, and therefore the acquisition of pulling does not acquire in them (based on Ri Migash, Bava Batra 76a).

once he brought out part of the object from the public domain, he acquired. In the acquisition of pulling, one must pull the object from the entire place where it was (above 3:3), and here the case is that he pulled the entire object from where it was in the public domain, but brought out only part of it into a private domain or a side alley. Although only part of the object was pulled into a domain where pulling is effective, his action is nevertheless considered a pulling that acquires (Maggid Mishneh).
a load of fruits. A load of fruit.
after he fixed the price. After they set the price, for before that their minds do not rely on the acquisition and the act of acquisition is ineffective (as below, halakhah 11).
and likewise if the buyer measured them in the public domain. After the price was fixed.
he acquired each one in turn by lifting. Each fruit that he took and lifted in order to measure it, he acquired.
the seller measures into the buyer's vessel. He measures and puts into the buyer's vessel, and the buyer himself did not lift them.
for the buyer's vessel does not acquire for him in the public domain. As above, halakhah 1.
once the seller accepted to sell. He agreed to the sale.
the buyer acquired. By the law of the acquisition of a courtyard (for the conditions of this acquisition see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:8-9, and see below 29:10).
in a domain where they are deposited with him. A third party, with whom the seller deposited the fruit.
that he remove them from his domain by renting their place. That he rent the place of the fruit, and they will be considered as being in his domain.
as we have explained. Above 3:7.
and the seller began to measure into the seller's vessel. And the measuring vessel is also the seller's.
a kor for thirty sela. A kor is a large measure of volume, containing thirty se'ah.
he can retract... since the fruit is still in his vessel and he has not finished the entire measure. But if he finished the entire measure he cannot retract, as explained in the next paragraph.

and the seller's vessel does not acquire for the buyer even though it is in the buyer's domain. As above, halakhah 2 (but if the fruit was placed in the buyer's vessel he acquired even if the measuring was not completed, as above, halakhah 1).
and if he said to him: a kor, thirty se'ah for a sela, each one in turn acquires, etc.. In this case each se'ah is considered by itself.

its sale is completed, since the fruit is neither in the seller's domain nor in the public domain. Since the fruit is in domains in which the buyer can acquire when it is in his vessel, the buyer acquires it through the seller's measuring, even though it is in the seller's vessel. As for the reason for this, some explained that by completing the measuring, it is as if he says to the buyer 'go and acquire with this vessel,' for just as lending a place is effective with the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain (above, halakhah 1), so lending the vessel is effective with the seller's vessel in the buyer's domain (Kesef Mishneh and others). Others explained that since the seller empties the measured fruit from his vessel for the purpose of the sale, they are acquired by the buyer even though they did not enter a vessel of his ('acquisition by measuring' - Mirkevet HaMishneh).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 6, that a buyer's vessels acquire for him even if there was no measuring.
and the measure belonged to a broker. Belonging to a third party, the intermediary.

once the measure was filled they are in the buyer's possession. In this case, since the measuring vessel belongs to the broker, the buyer acquires the goods while still in the measuring vessel (unlike the previous halakhah, where the acquisition was made only after they emptied the measuring vessel for the sale - see Kesef Mishneh, Mirkevet HaMishneh).
and the measure belongs to neither of them. But to a third party (a broker), as explained in the previous halakhah.
if the measure belonged to one of them. To the seller or the buyer, in a case where the fruit was sold in a domain in which the buyer can acquire.
markings. Notches, marks on the measure.
once he reached one of the markings, he acquired each one in turn, etc.. Like the law of filling the measure, which acquires (above, halakhah 8).

for the measure belongs to one of them and he relies on the markings on it. But if the measure belonged to another person (a broker), the seller does not rely on the markings, and the buyer acquires only if the measure is completely full.
fixed the price. Set the price.
until he lifts after he fixed the price. For they do not firmly decide to complete the acquisition until the price is known.
fixed and known. Set, so that the seller need not fix their price.
in the other ways by which movable property is acquired. The other methods used for acquisition.
one who pulls donkeys and laborers, etc.. He pulled the donkey drivers or the laborers loaded with goods into his domain, in order to acquire them.
even if the buyer himself was the one measuring. So that he in effect lifted the goods by his measuring.

both of them can retract. In the first case the buyer measured before the price was fixed, and in the second case the seller measured and the buyer performed no act of acquisition (however, if the buyer measured after fixing the price, he acquired, for the measuring is like lifting, as above, halakhah 5).
the buyer unloaded them and brought them into his house. The goods off the donkeys and laborers, while they were still in the seller's vessels.
if he fixed the price and afterward the seller measured, neither of them can retract. For now an effective acquisition has been made in them (as above, halakhah 7).
for his mind had not yet relied on selling. As long as the price was not fixed.
to inspect it. To examine it before he buys it.
if its price was fixed. Its price is set and known, and it is acquired immediately by lifting if he wants to buy it (above, halakhah 12).
and it was damaged in his hand. That vessel suffered damage, by accident and without the intent of the one who lifted it.
he is liable for its price. He must pay the seller the price of the vessel.
from the time he lifted it, it became his. For he performed an act of acquisition with it.
in order to acquire all of it. That he intends it to be entirely his if it pleases him.
and the item sold is dear to the buyer. In such a case there is no doubt that he lifted it for the purpose of acquisition.
that the seller is disgusted with it. Wants to be rid of it.
or he told another to lift it for him, or to pull it for him, or to take possession for him. To perform the act of acquisition on his behalf.
he acquired for him, and likewise with the other ways of transfer. For a person's agent is like himself (see also Hilchot Shelichin VeShutafin 1:1).

even though they are particular about the value, etc.. Although they exchanged on the basis of an assessment of their monetary value, they are not considered like money, which does not acquire movable property.

once one pulled or lifted, the other acquired the other movable property wherever it is. For the acquisition is made as an exchange of one thing for another, and when the first acquires one of them the other item is acquired by the other person (this method of acquisition is called 'chalifin' or 'exchange' - see below 6:2, 13:2, and see further below, halakhah 5).
he exchanged a donkey for a cow and a lamb. Reuven's donkey for Shimon's cow and lamb, so that when Reuven pulls the cow and lamb and acquires them, Shimon acquires the donkey.
he did not acquire. Neither the lamb nor even the cow that he pulled (Meiri, Bava Metzia 47a), and Shimon did not acquire the donkey.
who scooped. Took with his cupped hands.
by estimate. By approximation.
he acquired. By the acquisition of exchange; but if there is a difference between the market price of the object and the money he gave, it must be returned (below 13:2).

for this is something uncommon. A sale of this kind is not common, so the Sages did not require pulling of the movable property in it, but when one receives the money into his hand, his fellow acquires the movable property wherever it is.
and Shimon acquired the movable property. By pulling or lifting.
Reuven acquired the movable property wherever it is. For Reuven's waiving the fifty zuz is considered the giving of payment (see below 7:4; and see Even HaEzel here).
he did not acquire until he lifts or pulls. For such a sale is common, and therefore waiving the debt (which is considered giving payment) does not complete the acquisition.
and slaves. Canaanite slaves (see also Hilchot Avadim 5:1).
and all other movable property. But a coin is not acquired by exchange (below 6:1).

is acquired by exchange, and this is called 'kinyan', etc.. The term 'chalifin' has two meanings: one is the exchange of things of equal value (as explained in the previous halakhot). The other, called everywhere simply 'kinyan', is based on the idea of exchange, but unlike the first meaning it refers to an ordinary purchase for money, except that the item being bought is not before the parties to the transaction and they wish to complete the deal. For this the buyer gives the seller a symbolic object (as detailed in the next halakhah), and when the seller lifts it, the buyer acquires the thing he wants to buy. Usually the seller returns to the buyer that same symbolic object, since giving it was only for the purpose of effecting the transfer (see below, halakhah 7). This acquisition, which the Rambam calls simply 'kinyan', is called by the Rishonim 'kinyan sudar' (see, for example, Rashi, Kiddushin 3a, s.v. chalifin), because it is customarily done by lifting a sudar (a garment). For various cases in which kinyan sudar is used, see below, halakhot 11-13 and the explanation there.
with a vessel. With an object meant for a particular use.
with something forbidden for benefit. For example, an idolatrous vessel (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:2).
and not with fruit. Because they do not last like a vessel.

and not with a coin. Since it is customary to treat a coin according to the value stamped on it by the local authority and not according to its intrinsic value as metal, and the acquisition of exchange is made only with something of intrinsic value (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 45b and the Rishonim there, and Commentary on the Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:6).
but with the buyer's vessel. For the acquisition is made by the seller acquiring the vessel, and thereby he transfers the thing he is selling.
he acquired for the buyer. On behalf of the buyer.

for a gift given on condition that it be returned is called a gift. A gift given on condition that it be returned is considered a gift (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:9), and therefore it is effective for the acquisition of exchange.
the size of three fingerbreadths. A piece of cloth three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths.
as we have explained regarding the impurity of garments. Hilchot Kelim 22:1; and it was explained there that a piece of cloth torn from a garment becomes impure at this measure.
to exclude the seller's vessel. For 'to acquire with it' implies that the seller acquires the vessel.
but the seller... does not need witnesses. As above 1:2 (and see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:4 regarding the giver, and Hilchot Sechirut 2:8 regarding the renter or lender).
except for the one who denies. When one of the parties denies, and it must be determined who is right.
for they acquired from his hand. That they gave him a sudar to lift in order that he acquire a certain thing.

which is not the case with the other ways of transfer. With other methods of acquisition the parties may not retract after the acquisition even if they are still engaged in the same matter, since the other acquisitions are made on the thing acquired itself, and thus in the act of acquisition there is firm decision of mind from both parties. But in kinyan sudar there is no actual transfer of a thing from one person to another, and sometimes it is done during negotiations before they have finally agreed on all the details, and therefore there is no firm decision of mind from the parties and they can retract until they finish dealing with the matter (see Rashbam, Bava Batra 114a, Nimukei Yosef there 52b in the pages of the Rif).

which do not require an acquisition and for which an acquisition has no reason. For in these matters there is no transfer of particular property as in a sale, and therefore no acquisition is needed for these acts to take effect.
one who appoints an agent. Appoints an agent to perform an acquisitive act for him; the appointment can take effect by speech alone (Hilchot Shelichin VeShutafin 1:1).

one who delivers a protest or one who cancels a protest. Declares before witnesses that an acquisitive act he is about to do (such as a sale or the giving of a get) is being done against his will and therefore will have no validity (below 10:1). Or announces that all the protests he delivered are void (below 10:8, and see also Hilchot Gerushin 6:19-20).
one who waives a claim against his fellow. See also Hilchot Ishut 17:19.

most places were accustomed to confirm some of these things. In order to give force to the matters, it became customary for the one who does them to lift a sudar, thereby confirming the act he performed.
and we have acquired from so-and-so that so-and-so made so-and-so an agent. That the appointer lifted a sudar, thereby giving the agent the authority to perform the agency on his behalf.

this acquisition that they are accustomed to make in these matters serves only to show that he is not saying these words in jest or mockery. The reference is to acts like those mentioned above, halakhah 11, which take effect without needing an act of acquisition to give them force, and the purpose of the acquisition in them is to express the seriousness of the person regarding the act. There are indeed legal obligations in monetary matters that take effect and bind the person only if an acquisition by kinyan sudar was made on them (see, for example, Hilchot Shekhenim 11:4, 14:2, Hilchot Sechirut 2:1, Hilchot Sanhedrin 7:2-5, and many others).

matters that have no substance, an acquisition is of no use in them at all. In the examples mentioned in the previous halakhot, the discussion was of matters where the act or obligation itself has legal force, and the acquisition is made to give them additional force. But in the examples mentioned here, the obligation has no legal force at all, and therefore an acquisition in them is also nothing.

that they divide the courtyard between them. That is shared by them (see Hilchot Shekhenim 2:10; however, see there that if they defined the boundaries of the courtyard that each would receive and made an acquisition on it, the acquisition takes effect and they cannot retract).
that they both be partners in a trade. That they share between them the profits they make from their craft (see Hilchot Shelichin VeShutafin 4:2).
this is an acquisition of words and is of no use at all. Since these are mere words with no force, an acquisition on them has no effect either.

he did not transfer to his fellow any specific, known thing, neither the principal nor the fruit of a known principal. He did not transfer to him anything defined, neither in a way that transfers the thing itself ('principal'), nor in a way that transfers it for the eating of its fruit or its use ('fruit of a known principal', see below 23:1-2).
with which one does not acquire. One does not make a kinyan sudar with them.
as we have explained. Above 5:6.
are acquired by kinyan. They can be acquired by kinyan sudar (and they can also be exchanged for one another, as explained above 5:1 regarding wine and oil).
just as one does not acquire with it, so it is not acquired by kinyan. Just as one cannot make a kinyan sudar with it (as explained above 5:6), so it cannot be acquired by kinyan sudar.
tongues of gold and silver. Pieces that have no coin shape.
like ingots. Large lumps of raw material.
and are acquired by kinyan, and they acquire one another by exchange, as we have explained. Above 5:5 (acquired by kinyan), 5:1 (acquire by exchange).
all of them are money relative to other movable property. All these types of coins are considered money relative to other movable property.
as payment for movable property. As payment for movable goods.
he did not acquire until he lifts or pulls. The transaction is not completed by giving the payment, but by lifting or pulling the movable property.
as we have explained. Above 3:1.
and none of them is acquired by kinyan or serves to make a kinyan. It cannot be acquired by kinyan sudar, and one cannot make a kinyan sudar with it.
in what case does this apply. That gold and copper are considered money.
but gold dinars, etc.. Silver coins are the coins that mostly serve as money, and relative to them gold or copper coins are considered merchandise, as explained in the next halakhah.

he gave him a gold dinar, etc.. A person who received his fellow's gold dinar in exchange for twenty-five silver dinars is obligated to give him the silver dinars, and both parties may not retract, like a buyer who lifts or pulls merchandise and commits to pay, thereby completing the transaction (as above 3:4).
if new. If they agreed on new dinars that are not worn.
and if old. If they agreed on old dinars, which have the advantage of having already been found to be good coins for trade.

but if he gave him twenty-five silver, etc.. If the owner of the gold received the silver dinars and had not yet given the gold, the transaction is not yet complete, like a seller who received money while the buyer has not yet received the merchandise.
that the government or the province invalidated. That the king decreed that these coins no longer be used, or that the people of the country do not want to use them.
that do not circulate in that country. That one cannot trade with them in this country but only in another country.
and are acquired by kinyan. Kinyan sudar.

and the coins acquire, but the coins are not acquired by them. When a person buys bad coins from his fellow for payment, by lifting or pulling the bad coins the sale is completed and the payment is acquired by the seller. But lifting or pulling the payment does not complete the sale and does not transfer the bad coins to the buyer.
a coin has no way for one who is not in possession of it to acquire it. It is not possible to transfer ownership of a coin when the coin is in another place and the recipient cannot lift it.
except by means of the land. By the acquisition 'by means of land', as above 3:8.
and along with it. Together with it.
or that he rent the place of the money. In which case he acquires the money by the acquisition of a courtyard (above 3:7).
who had a debt owed by Shimon. That Shimon owes him money and they did not write a deed (but if they wrote a deed, the deed can be transferred by means of land, as below, halakhah 14).

that he did not acquire the debt. Because a monetary debt does not rest on specific coins in Shimon's hand but on Shimon himself, and there is no substantial thing here that can be transferred with the land (Maggid Mishneh).
the three of them were standing. Present at the time of the statement.

and none of the three can retract. For example, Reuven owed money to Levi, and had a debt or deposit in Shimon's hand, and Reuven instructed Shimon to give what he owed to Levi. In this case the money is acquired by Levi through Reuven's statement, and Reuven cannot retract and ask Shimon for the debt or deposit, and Levi too cannot claim his money from Reuven (see also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:3).

a halakhah without a reason. The manner of transfer is not understood, for no act of acquisition was performed but only words. However, the Rishonim (on Gittin 14a) explained in various ways why the Sages instituted this, for example, in order to ease the transfer of payments from person to person.
one does not learn from it to another law. For it is an exceptional halakhah, and applies only in the manner detailed here.
Reuven owed, etc.. Unlike the previous halakhah, here the giver asks a person who owes him nothing to pay his debt.
until I give you. I will repay you what you give to Shimon.
and Shimon accepted. Agreed to receive from Levi instead of from Reuven.

each of the three can retract. If Levi has not yet fulfilled Reuven's request, he can retract and say that he does not wish to give to Shimon, and Shimon can retract and say that he does not wish to collect from Levi, and Reuven can say that he will pay the debt himself.
and even if Levi paid Shimon part of his debt. Each can retract regarding the rest of the debt.
if Levi did not pay Shimon. The entire debt but only part of it.
and he claims Reuven for the rest of his debt. But what he received from Levi he cannot claim from Reuven (see also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 16:4).
one who sells a promissory note to his fellow. Reuven who wishes to sell Shimon a promissory note proving that Levi owes him money.
for he sold only the proof contained in it. Shimon is not interested in the note itself but in the proof that the note gives to its holder.
and the proof cannot be grasped by hand. It cannot be transferred by handing over from hand to hand.

that the transferor write to him: acquire such-and-such deed and every lien in it. The content of the deed ('the lien in it') can be transferred only through writing, in that the transferor writes to the buyer, on the deed itself or on another paper, that he transfers to him all the content the deed represents (see Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 66:1-2).
and hand over the deed to him. In addition, the deed itself must be handed over to him, for the physical deed is acquired not by writing but by handing over (see there).

and he does not need witnesses regarding his acquisition. If the owner of the original deed claims that he did not sell the deed, the holder of the deed need not bring witnesses that he acquired, since he is in possession of the deed (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 16:7, and see also Hilchot Nachalot 9:9-10).

but he needs witnesses regarding the claim. If the debtor contests that the holder of the deed actually acquired it validly from the original owner of the deed, the holder must bring proof, for since he wants to extract money from the debtor, the burden of proof is on him.
for he is my creditor. A person to whom I owe money.

but only the physical thing acquired. Only a substantial thing, so it turns out that by Torah law the buyer acquired only the physical deed, while the right to collect the debt still belongs to the seller.

one who sells a promissory note to his fellow can still waive it. He may forgive the borrower the debt. But in this case he must pay the buyer the value of the debt, since he caused him a loss in that he cannot collect the debt written in the deed (Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:10).

and even his heir can waive it. Even the heir of the seller may forgive the borrower, since by Torah law the right of collection belongs to him (and he too must pay the buyer - there; and see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 10:2, that if the deed was given as a gift of a person on his deathbed, the heir cannot waive it).
a woman who brought in. That she brought with her from her father's house.
for her hand is like his hand. For after she married, the husband has rights in her property.
along with it. Together with it.
he acquired the deed wherever it is. As with all movable property acquired by means of land (see above 3:9).
and wrote the deed. As evidence of the sale.
and the buyer is not with him. And it is permitted to do so (see below 30:1).
one who says, etc.. An owner of a field who appointed agents to acquire the field on behalf of another person and to write him a deed for the gift.
and the one acquiring for him took possession of the land. The agent took possession of the land to acquire it for the recipient of the gift.

the giver may retract regarding the deed, etc.. As long as the recipient has not received the deed, the giver may retract the appointment of agency for writing the deed, although he cannot retract the giving of the field, which has already been acquired by the recipient. It turns out, then, that the recipient will hold the field without a deed.

he may retract in this and in that. Since he made the acquisition of the field depend on the writing of the deed (see Maggid Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh that these laws are true also for a seller and buyer, since they were brought here in Hilchot Mechira).
as we have explained. Above 3:1.
did not act as the upright of Israel. Does not behave as the upright in Israel do.
gave only the deposit. Paid part of the price as an advance.
curse. Curse.
one who does not stand by his word. Who cancels a transaction after money was given (for one who retracts from an agreement made by words alone see below, halakhah 8).
the money is with him. With the seller.
were stolen or lost, he is not liable for their security. Like an unpaid custodian (see Hilchot Sheelah UFikadon 4:1).
it is as if he gave the money now. When he waives the debt in exchange for the barrel, it is considered as if he pays for it now (see above 5:4).

if he sold him land for his debt. Land is acquired with money alone in a place where they do not write a deed (see above 1:4; however, Or Sameach wrote that in this case no deed is needed in any event).

even though the loan money is not on hand at the time of the sale. Even if the borrower spent it, nevertheless when the lender acquires the land in exchange for the debt, it is considered as if he now gave the borrower money.
one who buys from his fellow, etc.. A person who wants to buy and has not yet performed an act of acquisition in the purchase.
and they fixed the price. They agreed on the price.
and he left a pledge for the price. An object as security that he will pay the price.
and he is not obligated to accept 'He who exacted payment'. Because giving a pledge is not like giving money.
he sold to him by words alone. They agreed orally on the sale.
in the way we have explained regarding taking possession. Above 1:8, 2.
and pulling. Above 2:6.
one who negotiates by words alone. Who committed himself to a transaction by a promise alone.
of those lacking faith. He has been guilty of a breach of trust.
and left his fellow's money with him, etc.. The agent did not use his fellow's money, and instead bought with his own money for himself the thing he was asked to buy for his fellow.
he is among the swindlers. And he is called wicked (Hilchot Ishut 9:17).
and he must go back and inform him. Inform the sender, to remove himself from the category of swindlers.
lest someone come and get there first to buy. Until he informs the one who sent him.
because he charged them to himself as a loan. That he took them for himself as a loan and undertook to return other money to his fellow.
and they accept it from him. They believe him.

as will be explained in the law of the business venture. In Hilchot Shelichin VeShutafin 7:4-6, regarding a person who received money from his fellow to do business and trade with it, that he must fulfill his mission and give the owner of the money a share of the profits as they agreed.
tied up and sealed. That each one gave his money in a tied bundle, or in another way so that it can be distinguished which money belongs to each (Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat 184).
and he kept going in and out demanding the rest of the money. The seller kept chasing after the buyer to give him the rest of the money.

the buyer did not acquire any of it. He did not acquire even a little of the field, because the seller revealed his intent that he does not transfer until he receives all the money (see below, halakhah 3).
the zivurit. Poor-quality land.
he sold his field because of its poor quality. Because the field was poor. In this case the seller wants to complete the acquisition as quickly as possible so that the buyer cannot retract.
even though he pulled, etc.. Even though an acquisition was made properly, if the seller chases after the rest of the money the acquisition is not completed.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 2.
he bought what is worth one hundred for two hundred. The buyer agreed to pay an inflated price.
because he sold at a high price. And fears that the buyer might retract.

and if the seller seized from the merchandise he sold an amount corresponding to the money that remained owing to him. If the seller took from the buyer's hand part of the thing sold, to the value of the amount not yet paid.
it is not taken from his hand. According to the law in monetary doubt (see above 3:10).
the merchandise is acquired. See also below 15:2.
and they made a kinyan from his hand on this. By kinyan sudar, to give force to his commitment (see above 5:11-13).
a maneh. One hundred zuz.
that he be selling of his own will first. When the owner of the field said 'when I sell,' he meant an ordinary sale made of full will and not under compulsion.
like one who was compelled and sold. And his commitment to sell to the first person does not apply in such a situation.
for what a court of three will assess it. As they will assess its value in a session of three people.
even according to two of the three. If two of them agreed on a certain value, that is sufficient, since his wording implies that he meant a court, and a court's assessment is determined by majority.
until all three say. For he did not mean a court's assessment, but what all three will say.
until all four assess and agree. Since he said four, which is more than a court, he did not mean a court's decision but specifically the agreement of four.

and sell it to one at what they agreed, and afterward the first one will acquire. When he sold to another person at the price they assessed the field, it is acquired by the first, as he stipulated with him. But if he sold to another person for more than they assessed, the latter acquired (as above, halakhah 7).
three or four. As the seller stipulated.

for they made a kinyan from his hand at the outset that he sold from now. For the seller's condition was fulfilled, and the buyer made a kinyan with him that the field is acquired by him from the time of the kinyan if the condition is fulfilled.
the treasurer. The one in charge of the property of the Temple.

for a statement to the Most High is like a transfer to a layman. One cannot retract from a statement regarding consecrated property, just as one cannot retract after an acquisition by handing over in an ordinary sale, and therefore he is obligated to sell to the consecrated property at the price originally stated (see Yad HaMelech and Even HaEzel).
if they became more expensive. If in the meantime the fruit became more expensive.
he acquired by Torah law. The fruit is acquired by the consecrated property on the basis of the giving of the money, since by Torah law money acquires even before pulling (above 3:1).

he may retract, for he has not pulled, and a layman's power shall not exceed, etc.. The treasurer may retract from the transaction, for in an ordinary sale the parties may retract after the money is given and before the acquisition of pulling (above 3:4), and the right of an ordinary person cannot be greater than the right of the consecrated property.
if he sold. The treasurer.

he acquired, for a layman's power shall not exceed, etc.. The buyer cannot retract, as in an ordinary sale where one cannot retract after pulling, and he must pay the value of the object at the time of the pulling.
he may retract. The treasurer.

as it is said: and he shall give the money and it shall be established for him. The verse reads: 'and he shall add a fifth of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall be established for him' (Leviticus 27:19), and the quotation here follows the wording of the Tosefta, Arakhin 4:4 (according to the version in the manuscripts and the first printing), and similarly in the Babylonian Talmud in several places (for example, Berakhot 47b, Shabbat 128a, and see Tosafot there, s.v. 'and he shall give the money').

and the treasurer is not obligated to accept 'He who exacted payment'. A treasurer who retracts after money was given or after pulling does not receive 'He who exacted payment' (unlike a layman who after pulling cannot retract at all, and after giving of money can retract and receive 'He who exacted payment' as above 7:1; and compare the laws here to Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 7:13, where it is explained that where the treasurer is the seller, giving of money before pulling binds both parties and even the treasurer cannot retract - and see Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh here, who proposed explanations for the distinction between the cases).

the property of minor orphans is like consecrated property. The Sages enacted for the benefit of the orphans that in certain cases they have the same law as consecrated property regarding the possibility of canceling the transaction.

for the property of orphans is acquired only with money, like consecrated property. In practice this is the only case where they have the law of consecrated property, but in the other cases mentioned below the law of orphans is the same as that of any other person (Kesef Mishneh).

if the fruit became cheaper, a layman's power shall not exceed theirs. Just as one who buys from anyone cannot retract after pulling and must pay for the fruit according to their value at the time of the sale, so too one who buys from orphans.
they may retract like other laymen. As for 'He who exacted payment,' it is explained below 29:8 that a minor does not receive 'He who exacted payment.'
for if we obligate them to take the fruit by Torah law. By the Torah law that money acquires.

they would not find anyone to give them money. For a person does not want to pay before receiving the merchandise and to be unilaterally obligated to the seller when the seller is not obligated to him. True, in the case where the buyer pulled the fruit from the orphans, it was explained above that the orphans may retract and not the buyer, but there the Sages did not worry that the orphans would not find buyers, because the delay in completing the transaction stems from the buyer, who has not yet paid (Mishneh Lamelech).

a layman's power shall not be greater than theirs. One who sells to orphans cannot retract after pulling, as in any sale, but receives from the orphans the price of the fruit at the cheap price of the time of the pulling.
they do not retract. Rather, they must pay the high price of the time of the pulling.
they would not find anyone to sell to them. On credit, for sellers would worry that the fruit might become cheaper by the time of payment.

the seller would say to them: the fruit was burned, etc.. But regarding consecrated property it was stated above, halakhah 2, that the seller cannot retract, and there is no concern that he would say the fruit was burned, since responsibility for fruit acquired by the consecrated property was placed on the seller because of the severity of consecrated property (Lechem Mishneh).
seasons. Times.
they upheld their words on the law of the Torah. The Sages left the law as the Torah law, that money acquires and not pulling.
with meat. In the sale of meat.

the last festival day of the festival. Shemini Atzeret, which is called the last festival day of the festival of Sukkot. Because it is a festival in its own right, people increase joy and meat on it (Rashi, Chullin 83a; but on the eve of the first day of Sukkot they are busy with the commandments of the festival and have no time to increase slaughter - Tosafot there).
Atzeret. Shavuot.
to the butcher. The slaughterer.
and took one dinar from the buyer in order to give him meat when he slaughters. He received a dinar from the buyer in exchange for a piece of meat worth a dinar from the slaughtered ox.
and the entire price of the ox was not collected. The butcher had not yet found buyers for all the meat of the ox.

he cannot retract, but they force the butcher to slaughter against his will. He cannot return the dinar to the buyer, but they compel the butcher to slaughter and to give the buyer his share of the meat.
if the ox died. Before he managed to slaughter it properly, and the meat became a carcass and is not kosher for eating.
it died in the buyer's possession. The piece of meat is considered to have become a carcass in the buyer's possession and he bears the loss.
even if they hung him. In order to torment him into agreeing to sell.
for because of his duress he made a firm decision and transferred. He fully agreed to transfer because of the duress, in exchange for receiving the money.

even though he did not take the money before witnesses. The witnesses did not see the transfer of the money, but he admitted that he received money, and from this we know that in the end he consented to sell.
delivered a protest. A declaration that the sale will be made without his consent, and he cancels it in advance.
they take it from his hand. From the buyer's hand, for possession of land for several years does not prove ownership for one who is considered a robber of the field (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 13:11).
and the witnesses must know that he sells because of the duress, etc.. That they know the details of the case and know that he was truly compelled to sell.

one who makes a compromise. A claimant who was forced to make a compromise with the defendant in court, and before they made the compromise with him he delivered a protest before witnesses that he does so against his will (see Ri Migash, Bava Batra 40a, Responsa of the Rambam 250).
by waiver. Forgoing a debt.

for in a gift one follows only the revealed intent of the giver, etc.. The giving of a gift is based on the free and complete will of the giver, since he receives nothing in return, and if there is no complete will the gift is void (see also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 5:4).
who frightened him with something he is able to do. He threatened him with something that the oppressor is capable of doing.
and the lessor held no deed. Stating that the orchard was leased to the holder, and which proves the lessor's ownership of the field.
that the lessee ate. He held the orchard and ate its fruit.
I will hide my lease deed. I will conceal the lease deed in my possession.
and I will claim that it was bought by me. For one who holds land for three years can claim that he bought it even though he has no deed of ownership (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 11:2).
and claimed that the orchard is his. The lessee claimed that the orchard belongs to him.
and afterward the lessor delivered a protest. Before the same witnesses who saw the lessee deny it in court, that the sale he will make to the lessee is only because he threatened him.

for he has witnesses that he is under duress, etc.. It is necessary that the witnesses of the protest know that the seller is under duress (above, halakhah 2), and since the witnesses of the protest know that the lessee denied him and claimed that the orchard is his, this proves that the sale was made under duress.
in what case does this apply. That the sale is not void until the seller delivers a protest.
the seller need not deliver a protest. Since it is known that this is robbery from him, it is to be assumed that he sold it to him out of fear.
as we have explained in Hilchot Gezelah. 9:16.
they may. They are permitted.
in that same sale. In the deed of sale.

and this is nothing. This does not detract from the validity of the protest. The same applies if they testified orally that a protest was delivered to them regarding the sale deed on which they signed (see Hilchot Edut 3:8).
and likewise if he admitted before them, etc.. See also Hilchot Gezelah 9:14-15.
he is not obligated to return anything. If he claims that his admission was under compulsion, and in fact he received no money.
they already knew that he is under duress. From the time he delivered the protest to them.
he counted the money before them. They saw with their own eyes that he received money from the oppressor.

and if he said to the witnesses of the protest, etc.. Just as one can deliver a protest about the sale itself, declaring that the sale he will make is not of his will, so one can deliver a protest about the cancellation of the first protest, declaring that the cancellation he will make is not of his will, since he never wants to transfer to this oppressor. This is a 'protest of a protest,' which in practice reinforces the first protest and establishes that it is never void, and therefore the sale is void.
for any kinyan that I take to cancel the protest and the protest of the protest. If I agree to lift a sudar as a kinyan to the effect that I cancel the protest or the protest of the protest.
in the manner we have explained. Above 5:12-13, that a kinyan is made to make known that the matter is done with firm decision.

and stipulated conditions that can be fulfilled. For if he stipulated something that cannot be fulfilled, it is as if he speaks exaggerated and hyperbolic words with no substance, and the condition is void (see Hilchot Ishut 6:1, 6:17).

and we have already explained the laws of conditions in Hilchot Ishut. The laws of conditions are explained there in chapter 6, and they apply to the laws of betrothal and divorce and to all monetary laws (there, halakhah 1, and see there halakhah 14; and see also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:6-8 regarding the giving of a gift).

even though the condition was fulfilled, he did not acquire, for this is an asmakhta. An asmakhta is an obligation dependent on a future condition, and it has no acquisitive force because the transferor thinks the condition will not be fulfilled and does not firmly decide in his mind to transfer.

and this one took possession of the house from now, he has acquired, etc.. In the case discussed here, there is no commitment to a future acquisition, but the acquisition made now depends on a future condition. And since he already transferred to him from now, it is not an asmakhta, for there is firm decision of mind, and when the condition is fulfilled the acquisition takes effect.
on that day. On the particular day mentioned in the condition.

even if he took possession of the house after the condition was fulfilled, he did not acquire, for this is an asmakhta. For his taking possession of the house is based on a transfer in the manner of an asmakhta, which is not whole-hearted.

one who gives a deposit to his fellow... my deposit is forfeited to you. A buyer who gave the seller money as a commitment that he will buy a certain thing from him, and told him that if he does not buy from him the money will remain in the seller's hand.
if I retract from you. If I back out of the commitment toward you.
and the other says to him. The seller says to the buyer.
I will double your deposit for you. I will give you double the amount you gave.
for it is in his hand. For the buyer already actually gave it to him, and this is proof that he transferred to him whole-heartedly.
who repaid part of his debt. A borrower who returned to the lender part of the amount of the loan.
and deposited the deed with a third party. The borrower asked that the deed be deposited with a third party so that the lender would not deny that part of the debt had been paid.

and said to him, etc.. The borrower undertook that if he does not repay the rest of the debt by a certain day, the deed will be returned to the lender and he will be able to collect the entire sum including the part already paid.
for his mind still relies that perhaps it will be or perhaps it will not. The transferor hopes and relies in his mind that the thing stipulated will occur in his favor and he will not need to give.
if I come from here until such-and-such a day, acquire this house from now. When I arrive before such-and-such a day it will become clear retroactively that the house is acquired by you from now.

and they made a kinyan from his hand on this. The transferor lifted a sudar to make known that he says these words whole-heartedly and not in jest or mockery (see above 5:13) (Kesef Mishneh in his second explanation).
that he is selling in order to go to such-and-such a place. That he wanted to move and live in another place.
or because rain was withheld, in order to buy wheat with the price of his courtyard. That wheat became expensive because of drought and he was forced to sell his property to buy it.
it is like selling on condition. Although he did not explicitly stipulate that the sale is conditional on his carrying out his plan, it is considered as if he stipulated it.
if rain fell... or wheat came and became cheap. And now he does not need to sell his courtyard in order to buy wheat.
the road was blocked to go to that land. It is impossible to reach it.
for he was not able to go up. He was prevented from moving by an obstacle related to himself, such as that he became ill (see Maggid Mishneh and Mishneh Lamelech).
and matters in the heart are not matters. What was not stated explicitly has no force (see, for example, Hilchot Ishut 8:2).
if he sold it or gave it to that so-and-so, he acquired. Retroactively.

that he will return the merchandise to him at such-and-such a time or when he gives him the money. That they agreed between them on a time known in advance when the buyer will give the seller the merchandise as a gift or for money (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 207:11, and according to his explanation the words 'at such-and-such a time' also apply to the words 'when he gives him the money,' and therefore this is a complete sale for a fixed time, unlike a loan, and there is no concern of interest, as below 23:5 and unlike the next halakhah; and see Me'irat Einayim and Even HaEzel, who explained differently).
and he will return it as he stipulated. As he stipulated.

the fruit belongs to the seller. When the seller stipulates this, it is not a sale but a loan, for at any moment the seller can return the money to the buyer and get his land back. And since the buyer did not acquire the land, he is forbidden to eat the fruit because of the prohibition of interest (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 207:11, and compare Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 6:5).
and there is no trace of interest in this. There is not even interest that is forbidden by rabbinic law.
for he obligated himself by his own will with this condition. For there is a complete sale on the seller's part, but the buyer undertook to sell it back in case the seller brings money.
the matter is close. It is to be assumed.

for the mind of this relative relied on the words of the agent, etc.. Although the agent did not answer the seller unequivocally that his relative would return the land after the money is given, the seller relies on this, so it turns out that he did not make a complete sale but the sale is conditional on the land returning to him when he has money, and this is not a sale, as explained in the previous halakhah. [Note: In the printed editions and some manuscripts the reading in the Rambam is: 'for the mind of this relative did not rely on the words of the agent, because he did not give him a clear answer.' According to this the commentators explained that the seller does not transfer anything because he wants to transfer only according to his condition and does not know whether the buyer agrees to this - see Lechem Mishneh and Even HaEzel, and see further Yalkut Shinuy Nusachot in the Frankel edition.]
for they made a kinyan from his hand on it. That he committed himself to it by kinyan sudar.
in a distinguished court. One that has ordained sages (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 10:5).
that he deposit his rights with the court. That he place in the court the deed proving his right, so that the matter is entrusted to the court and he cannot regret it.
that he not be under duress. For if duress occurs, the condition is void, as below, halakhah 14.
his receipt. A receipt, a document proving that the debt was paid.
without any condition at all. For if he committed himself conditionally it is only an asmakhta (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 25:8).

you are witnesses against me. And thereby he proves the seriousness of his intent. If he did not say so, even though he admitted before witnesses, he can claim that he did not intend to commit himself but to make a fool of his fellow (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 6:6-7).
as a guarantor obligates himself. Just as a guarantor obligates himself to pay a debt that is not his own (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 25:1-2).
and in this. In this manner.

and there is no known and available thing that he gave as a gift. And therefore he does not firmly decide in his mind to obligate himself to it (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 25:13 regarding a guarantor's obligation for an unspecified amount, and see also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:5).
and why, etc.. How can a person obligate himself of his own will to support his wife's daughter (see Hilchot Ishut 23:17), when this is not a fixed amount.

and the matter is similar to matters acquired by speech. A monetary commitment made at the time of betrothal between husband and wife or between in-laws is valid by speech alone without a kinyan, since because of the joy of the marriage they firmly decide in their minds to transfer by speech (there, halakhot 13-14). And for the same reason, when a person marries a woman he obligates himself even in an unspecified matter (see Kesef Mishneh).
they make a kinyan from this one that he owes that one one hundred dinars. And this is not an asmakhta, since he committed himself unconditionally, as above, halakhah 15.
they make a kinyan from this one... they make a kinyan from his creditor. These kinyanim are made to make known that the words are said whole-heartedly and not in jest or mockery (see above 5:13).
to overcharge. To deceive, and to buy or sell something not at its true value.
because it can be repaid. The difference in price can be returned, and any prohibition that can be remedied by payment is not punished by lashes (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
one-sixth exactly. Exactly one sixth.
for example, he sold what is worth six for five, or what is worth six for seven. That the difference in price, in favor of the seller or the buyer, is one sixth of the true value of the thing sold.
or what is worth five for six, or what is worth seven for six. That the difference in price is one sixth of the sum actually paid.
the purchase is acquired, and the one who overcharged must return the overcharge. The sale is not void, and the one who overcharged must return the difference to the one who was overcharged.
for example, he sold what is worth sixty dinars for fifty dinars and a perutah. Here the buyer overcharged the seller by slightly less than a sixth of the value of the item sold.

the one who overcharged him cannot retract if this one wished and accepted, even though the purchase is void. Although the difference in price is grounds for canceling the transaction, the overcharged party may nevertheless decide that he wants the transaction to stand and forgo the difference (Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh).
a perutah exactly. Exactly a perutah.
for there is no overcharge for perutot. An overcharge of exactly a perutah is not significant and is forgiven.
he may retract. He is entitled to retract.
until he can show it to a merchant or to his relative. Until enough time passes to show the merchandise to a merchant or a relative who is expert and knows the value of the merchandise.
he cannot retract. For presumably he forgave.
he may retract for overcharge. He claims the difference in price when it is exactly one sixth.
and needless to say for the cancellation of the sale. When the difference is more than a sixth.
until he sees one like the one that was sold. That he finds an item identical to the item he sold and ascertains its value from an expert.
that has no variation within its kind. That there is no difference between one and another.
all of it is of equal value. Its price is uniform.
that came into his hand like his sale. That merchandise similar to the one he sold came into the seller's hand, and he was overcharged in it.
that was a gold dinar, etc.. Whose rate was twenty-four silver dinars.
and exchanged it. Changed the gold dinar.
for twenty dinars or twenty-eight. Silver dinars, where the overcharge is exactly a sixth.
lacked a sixth. That a sixth of its weight was lost from use.
and they used to pass sela coins by count and not by weight. They count each sela as a unit and do not take into account the loss in its weight (and see below 15:1-2).
until the eves of Sabbaths. When people go to the market to buy Sabbath needs, and he can then show it to one who is expert.
if he was not familiar. A person expert in the value of the merchandise.
to the money-changer. A changer of money who is expert in assessing coins.
if he recognizes it. If the one who gave it identifies it.
he may return it. Like one who buys something with a defect, who may return it even after several years (below 15:3, and see Maggid Mishneh there).
to pass it with difficulty. That it circulates only with great difficulty.
he cannot return it after some time. If the one who overcharged does not want to accept it, the one overcharged cannot compel him after the time detailed above, halakhah 11, has passed.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 4.
and not the seller. Although he too loses, for he sold at five and now it is worth seven.
you could not retract. For the price rose after the merchandise passed into the buyer's possession.
for the purchase is acquired and he must return. For when the overcharge is exactly a sixth, the sale stands, and the overcharged party receives the difference (as above, halakhah 2).

and when it became more expensive, it became more expensive in the buyer's possession. Therefore, although the price is now higher than what the buyer paid, the seller pays the difference as of the time of the sale, because the rise in price occurred in the buyer's possession, and at the time he bought he was overcharged.
in armor. Metal plates that soldiers wear for protection.
one who buys with coins by estimate. A buyer who buys with coins by approximation.

even though he acquires by exchange, he has acquired, and returns the overcharge. Although the giving of the money acquires for him the cow wherever it is, by the law of exchange (above 5:3), nevertheless the law of overcharge applies to it, so that if the difference in price is a sixth, the sale stands and the difference is returned.
as we have explained. Above 12:2.
his household vessels. Those that are important to him, and which he sells only for a high price.
he would not have sold him his household vessels. And the buyer must take into account that the seller sells them for more than their true value (see below, halakhah 4).
that you have no overcharge claim against me. That you waive the overcharge in the sale.
for he does not know how much overcharge there is in it in order to waive it. And there is no waiver except of a known thing (see also below 15:6).
on condition that there be no overcharge in it. That he informs him that there is no overcharge in this sale.
for every monetary condition stands. For a person may waive what is due to him.
one who does business on trust. A merchant who tells buyers the price at which he bought the goods and what profit he makes on selling them.
he has no overcharge claim against him. Even if he sold at a price higher than the market price.
bought many vessels... in one purchase. That he bought at once vessels of different quality.

he may not calculate the bad ones on trust and the good ones at their value. He may not divide the purchase price among the number of vessels and calculate as if the price of all the vessels were uniform, and sell the poor ones on trust and the fine ones for more than that, at their value.
but either both on trust. That he sells them all for the same amount, so he makes a fixed profit on each item.
or both at their value. That he sells the poor ones cheaply and the fine ones dearly.
to add to the merchandise. To include in the price of the goods.
the porter. A carrier.
the donkey driver. Who transported the goods for him on the donkey.
the inn. Where he lodged on the way.
his own wages. His payment for his effort.
he does not add it to the merchandise. Because it is included in the profit he asks from the buyer.
a gentile has no overcharge claim. There is no obligation to return the overcharge to him (and regarding a gentile's mistake in buying and selling see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 11:4).
that which is acquired from hand to hand. Movable property, which can be transferred.
which were likened to land. They were equated in law with land (see Hilchot Genevah 2:2).
for their substance is acquired only for the proof they contain. They have no intrinsic value and serve only as proof.
an agent who erred by any amount. Who sold or bought for the sender at a mistaken price, even slightly.
it is void. The sender may cancel the transaction, for agency is only to improve and not to harm (Hilchot Shelichin VeShutafin 1:2).

with a guardian. A person appointed to look after the affairs of minors or others who cannot do so themselves. [Note: The vocalization of the word follows the Greek original. In the Commentary on the Mishnah in the Rambam's own handwriting there are several forms of vocalizing this word: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe is not vocalized).]

and he is not like a court because he is an individual. Even though he was appointed by a court, his law is that of an agent: the sale is void, and not like a court, whose sales carry waiver up to a sixth (as below, halakhah 10).
and they erred... whether in movable property or in land. Although generally there is no overcharge in land, it is the responsibility of the court to sell the land at its proper price.
if they erred by less than a sixth, it is a waiver like a layman. For the court has authority to waive up to a sixth, as if they were the seller himself.
if they erred by a sixth the sale is void. For the court is charged with selling the property at its value (and see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 12:11).
