and if they wished, etc.. That the court may decide whether to cancel the sale entirely, or to act as anyone else, where in an overcharge of a sixth the difference in price is returned.

a layman's power shall not be greater than the orphans'. And just as one who buys land or a slave from an ordinary person at such a price cannot retract (as above, halakhah 8), so too regarding orphans.
they are like purchasers. They are considered buyers from one another, for at first the joint property belonged to all of them together, and when they divide, each sells to the other his share.
and if they stipulated between them that they divide as the judges assess. That they agreed in advance to divide according to the law of a court that assesses and sells the property of orphans.
they are like other movable property. Although sometimes they have a special need, and people are willing to pay more than their price for them, nevertheless the law of overcharge applies to them.
except for four things that the Sages enumerated. Land, slaves, deeds, and consecrated property.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 9.
so too with the rental of land. For a lease is like a temporary sale (below, halakhah 17).
a hall. A spacious hall.
to work with him. To work for him for hire (for the law of a contractor see below, halakhah 18).
because it is like buying him for a time. As if he buys him as a slave for a limited period.
and slaves have no overcharge. As above, halakhah 8.
he hired him to sow land for him. He hired the worker to sow the field with an amount of seed suited to that land.
and witnesses came and testified that he sowed less than was fitting for it. And now it is impossible to add more seed to the field.

it is in doubt whether he has an overcharge claim because of the seed or has no overcharge claim because of the land. Some explained that the case is where the seed belongs to the worker, and the question is whether the seed is considered movable property, in which there is overcharge, or is subordinate to the land, in which case there is no overcharge (Lechem Mishneh). Others explain that the seed belongs to the householder, and the discussion concerns overcharge in the wages for the work: if he is considered a contractor for the seed there is overcharge, and if a contractor for the land there is no overcharge (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 227:62).

they administer to him only the oath of the court's imposition. If he has incurred an oath by Torah law, for example, by admitting part of the claim, they do not administer it to him, because one does not swear regarding land (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 5:1). But they do administer to him the heset oath that the Sages enacted for one who is sued and denies everything (there 1:3).

or more... he returns the overcharge. He returns the difference in price. And although an overcharge of more than a sixth cancels the sale (above 12:4), cancellation of the sale is not applicable here because the case is one where the renter already used the vessel or animal (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 227:64).
even after a long time. And the law of renting is not like that of selling, where the buyer can retract only within the time it takes to show the merchandise to a merchant or a relative (above 12:5).
and each of the two. Who was overcharged by the other party.
may always retract like the seller. He may claim the overcharge without time limit, like a seller (above 12:6).
we have already explained. Above 13:5.
permitted. Since he informed him and the buyer agreed.
to set prices. To fix prices.
and to appoint officers for this. To supervise commerce (and see further Hilchot Genevah 8:20).
necessities of life. Essential for human needs.
spices. Aromatics used in perfumes or seasonings.
the chamam. Some identify it with ginger, and some with cinnamon.
and costus and frankincense. Kinds of aromatics used in the incense (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 2:3-4).

and one who buys from him sells them only at cost. For the eggs must be sold directly to the consumer (see also in the next halakhah), and if the buyer nevertheless wants to sell to another buyer he must sell without profit.
to make a business. To buy from the owners in order to sell to others.
for the oil is abundant. And likewise other things (Meiri, Bava Batra 91a).
he is permitted to profit. For there is no concern that prices will rise.
one may not hoard produce. It is forbidden to hoard produce and refrain from selling it so that the price rises.
his own produce. His grain.

it is permitted to hoard produce for three years, etc.. It is permitted to buy produce in the sixth year of the Sabbatical cycle in order to sell it in that year, in the Sabbatical year, and in the year after it, because such hoarding benefits the public that suffers from a shortage of produce in the Sabbatical year and after it (Rashbam, Bava Batra 90b).
for he brings a curse into the prices. For everyone fears the shortage, and any fluctuation in the market may cause prices to rise.
a curse. A curse.
he is like one who lends at interest. For he exploits the distress in order to profit, like one who lends at interest.
and to take them out from place to place. Although it is forbidden to do so with produce that is a necessity of life, as mentioned in the next halakhah.
like other spices. Which do not have the restrictions stated here (see above, halakhah 2).
they do not export, etc.. So as not to cause a shortage and a rise in prices.
to fix. To set.
that no one other than one may do. That no one else engage in the same craft.
but if there is an important sage in it. Who is appointed over the public to repair the affairs of the province.
who did not accept the condition. Who did not agree to the content of the condition and violated it.

and anyone who lost because of the condition not with the sage's knowledge pays. One who punished and caused loss to the violator of the condition, where it was not with the sage's knowledge, must compensate him.
verbal wronging. The prohibition of causing distress to another person through speech.
he shall not say to him: remember your earlier deeds. See also Hilchot Teshuvah 7:8.
is not your fear your confidence. Fear of Heaven gives assurance that nothing bad will befall you, and had you been God-fearing these sufferings would not have come upon you.
remember, who that was innocent ever perished. Consider whether any person free of sin has perished, that is, had you been free of sin you would not be suffering.
who never sells grain. And so it turns out that he caused distress to the donkey drivers and to that man.
from this you learn that one who wrongs a convert. Verbally.
because of: you shall not wrong one another. The prohibition of verbal wronging of every Jew.
and because of: do not wrong one another. The prohibition of monetary overcharge toward every Jew (above 12:1), and see below, halakhah 17, the reason one violates this prohibition.

for the verse put both in the language of plain wronging. The verse dealing with verbal wronging among Jews and the verse dealing with monetary overcharge among Jews both use general language that includes all kinds of wronging. With regard to a Jew, one verse is interpreted as referring to verbal wronging and the other to monetary overcharge, but with regard to a convert this cannot be interpreted so, since verbal wronging already appears elsewhere explicitly ('and you shall not wrong a convert') as does monetary overcharge ('and you shall not oppress him'), and therefore with regard to a convert these verses are interpreted in their general meaning, so that with regard to a convert there are two general prohibitions and an additional prohibition for each type of wronging.
greater. More severe.
was given to be repaid. The money can be returned.

because the matter is entrusted to the heart. It depends on the intent of the one who wronged, for sometimes only the Lord knows whether he said the words in good faith or with intent to insult (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 4:10).
anything that is entrusted to the heart. See also Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:2.

and anyone who cries out because of verbal wronging is answered immediately, as it is said: for I am the Lord. I, the Lord, recognize the wronging and hear the one wronged. For the gates of wronging are always open (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a), and therefore the one wronged is answered immediately.

for overcharge applies only to money. The law of overcharge (detailed in chapters 12-13) applies only where they erred in assessing the value of the merchandise, where for less than a sixth people usually waive, because it is hard to assess the merchandise exactly, and for more than a sixth the sale is void because the whole transaction is based on a significant error.

but in calculation, he returns. If they erred in calculating the quantity of goods or the number of coins, he must return even for a small error of less than a sixth, and on the other hand the sale is not void even for an error of more than a sixth, because it is based on a correct assessment of the merchandise's value and the error occurred only in carrying out the transaction (Ri Migash, Bava Batra 90a).
and one hundred and one were found, or ninety-nine. The seller erred and gave him one nut more or fewer than they agreed.
the purchase is acquired and he returns the error. The buyer returns the excess or the seller makes up the shortage.
even after several years. Unlike the law of overcharge (compare above 12:5-7).

if the money was found to be more or less than the count they fixed, he returns. If the seller received more than the sum they agreed, he must return the difference to the buyer, and if the seller received less than the sum, the buyer must make it up.
for they made a kinyan from his hand. That he made a kinyan sudar to strengthen his words (see above 5:11-13).
for it is a kinyan made in error. For he thought he had received what was due to him.
for this is a purchase made in error. And therefore the whole sale is void, and the seller cannot return the difference and uphold the sale (see the next halakhah).
an isar. A small coin worth one twenty-fourth of a dinar.
he returns the vessel. The buyer may return the vessel and get his money back against the seller's will, because this is a purchase made in error.
the choice is in the seller's hand. The seller is not obligated to give the buyer the value of the loss.

either take it as it is, or take your money and go. The choice is yours whether to keep the merchandise and forgo the loss, or cancel the transaction on the claim of a purchase made in error and get your money back.
he does not return it unless he specified. Unless they agreed explicitly that if such a defect is found in it he will return the merchandise.
anyone who buys without specification. A person who buys without special agreement between him and the seller.
or until he says to him. The buyer.
like one who specifies in overcharge. Who does not waive the overcharge unless he knew its amount at the time of the waiver (above 13:3-4).
which are not noticeable. They are not visible except after examination.
but only to calm my mind. To soothe and set my mind at ease (based on Psalms 65:8), so that I would think that just as it does not have these defects it has no other defects.
she is lame. Limping, which is a visible defect.
she bites, she lies down. She is accustomed to bite and to lie down a lot, and these are defects that are not visible.

if she was lame... this is not a purchase made in error. Since he saw that she has one of the visible defects, he should have checked the other defects as well, and since he did not check, he waived them.
and such-and-such a defect and such-and-such a defect. The seller mentioned additional defects, but did not show them.

this is not a purchase made in error. For the buyer cannot claim 'I thought she had only the defect you showed me and you mentioned further defects only to calm my mind'; rather the buyer was obliged to check all the defects the seller mentioned (Kesef Mishneh).
with a severed hand. With an amputated arm.
epileptic. Suffering from epilepsy.
this is a purchase made in error. Because the buyer thought that just as she does not have the visible defects she does not have the hidden defects.
he has an overcharge claim against him. Even though he specified the overcharge (compare above 13:3).
since I saw that it is not worth a zuz. But much more.
for he intends only to calm my mind. To set my mind at ease so that when I see that it is worth more than a zuz I will think it is truly worth a hundred dinars.

until he specifies the amount of overcharge that there is in his purchase, either exactly or close to it, to the extent that the mind errs. The seller must inform the buyer of the exact value of the item, or its approximate value, such that the buyer takes his words seriously and knows what he is waiving.
and in this it is fitting for the judges to rule. In this manner the judges must judge.
he already saw it. And surely waived it.
a wart. A growth.

for slaves are not for use of the bed. And therefore they do not have the law of one who betroths a woman, where if one of these defects is found in her the betrothal may be annulled (Hilchot Ishut 7:7).
insane. Mad.
suffering. In pain.
an armed robber. An armed bandit.
registered for the kingdom. Listed in the king's records as bound to the king's service (Meiri, Bava Batra 92b).
a snatcher. A thief.
unless he specified. Unless the buyer explicitly stipulated that he intends to buy a slave who does not have these things.
for the seeds themselves are not eaten. Rather, what grows from them.
whose presumption is for sowing. Seeds of this kind are bought for sowing, and if they do not sprout it is a purchase made in error.
provided that they did not fail to sprout on their own account. That there is no visible reason why they did not sprout, and therefore it is to be assumed that the seeds are defective.
since people eat it. Some people.

and the same applies to things sold for medicine. That if they are used only for medicine or he informed him that he buys for medicine, and they did not help, the seller must return the money he received.

from here you learn, etc.. In the previous halakhot it was explained that when the seller knows the seed was bought for sowing and it did not sprout, he must return the buyer's money even though the seed is in the ground and the buyer cannot return it. From this one can learn regarding a buyer who took the merchandise to another country, as explained further on.
he cannot say to him. The seller to the buyer.
and the seller is occupied. Is busy.
and even if it was lost or stolen after he informed him. After the buyer informed the seller that there is a defect in the merchandise (see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh).
it is in the seller's possession. As if it was lost or stolen from the seller, and he must return the buyer's money.

one who buys merchandise and a defect is found in it, etc.. A person who buys merchandise with a flaw that is grounds for canceling the transaction - the transaction is void from the outset. However, as long as he has not returned the merchandise to the seller, he is responsible for it like a paid custodian (for if a person should come along who wants to buy the merchandise, he will sell it to him and receive payment - Be'er HaGolah in the name of the Bach). Therefore, if the merchandise is lost or stolen, the buyer loses his money that is with the seller, like a paid custodian who bears responsibility for theft and loss (Kiryat Melech Rav).
and if it became wormy and spoiled because of time. It spoiled and rotted.
it is in the seller's possession. The buyer is considered under duress and is not liable for the merchandise, so the seller loses and must return the buyer's money.
and if he could have informed the seller and did not inform him. If the buyer could have informed the seller that the merchandise was about to spoil and was negligent and did not inform him.
it is in the buyer's possession. For this is not duress and he must bear the responsibility (there).
one who sells an ox to his fellow and it is found to be a gorer. It turned out that it is accustomed to gore, and it must be slaughtered to prevent it from goring and it cannot be used for plowing.
where the buyer buys both for slaughter and for plowing. That the buyer is accustomed to buy both for slaughter and for plowing, for example, he sells meat and is also a farmer.
but if it was known that he buys only for plowing. Even if he did not say so explicitly, for example, a farmer who always buys for plowing.
if it became known for certain that it was a tereifah when he bought it. For an example of this see below 20:15.

he returns the slaughtered animal to him and the seller returns the money. And the seller cannot claim that he wants to receive a live animal back, since the buyer is a butcher whose practice is to slaughter.
and if he altered it and made another defect before the defect became known to him, etc.. If he made a defect that is not customarily made, he must pay the seller for this.
he returns the shreds to him. And he need not return a garment, since he used it in its ordinary use, as in the previous halakhah.

he sewed it and afterward the defect became known, etc.. A person who bought a garment and increased its value by sewing it, and afterward found a defect in it and wants to return it to the seller, is entitled to receive his money back from the seller, and in addition payment for the added value of the garment.

he returns all the fruit he ate. The buyer must pay the seller for the fruit he ate, since the sale was voided retroactively and it turns out that the fruit eaten belonged to the seller (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 232:33).
he must pay him rent. The buyer must pay the seller rent for the time he lived in his courtyard.
he returns the money. The seller returns the buyer's money.
molars. Teeth.
he swears the heset oath. Like one who denies a claim (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).

because the buyer should have examined the ox himself. A person who buys from a dealer knows that the dealer does not keep the merchandise with him and is not expert in its quality, and so the buyer must examine the merchandise himself (unlike the previous halakhah, which deals with an ordinary seller who knows the quality of the merchandise and must reveal to the buyer everything he knows).

one who slaughters a firstborn, etc.. A firstborn of a pure animal is holy and must be offered on the altar, but if a blemish befell it, it may be slaughtered and eaten. A firstborn is slaughtered only on the ruling of an expert who determined that this blemish permits the firstborn for slaughter, and if it was slaughtered without the ruling of an expert the firstborn is forbidden for eating and must be buried (Hilchot Bechorot 3:1-9).

whoever ate, ate, and he returns the money to him. Since he sold a forbidden thing, they penalized him to return the buyer's money, even the money for what the buyer already ate (see also Hilchot Bechorot 3:9).

he settles accounts with the butcher for the price of the tereifah, and the butcher returns the remainder to him. They assess the value of the tereifah, and the butcher gives the buyer the difference between the sum the buyer paid him and the value of the tereifah (for kosher meat is worth more than tereifah meat).
and they were found to be untithed produce. From which terumah and tithes had not been separated.
and it was found to be wine of libation. That had been poured out for idolatry.

and if he ate them, he ate, and the seller returns nothing to him. For with a prohibition of rabbinic law they did not penalize the seller to return the money (see Sma, Choshen Mishpat 234:3, Netivot HaMishpat there 4, Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 119:27, who explained in various ways the reason for the distinction between a Torah prohibition and a rabbinic one).

and all prohibitions of benefit, whether from the Torah or from their words. For example, chametz on Pesach, which is forbidden for benefit by Torah law, and on the eve of Pesach in the sixth hour is forbidden for benefit by rabbinic law.
and the law of sale does not apply to them at all. Because they have no value.
four measures among sellers. Four different laws in sale, regarding who may retract from the transaction.
he sold him fine wheat. They agreed between them on fine wheat.

the buyer may retract and not the seller. The buyer can claim that he wanted to buy fine wheat and this is a purchase made in error. But the seller cannot cancel the sale if the buyer does not wish to cancel it, since the buyer can argue against him that he forwent his loss and agreed to uphold the sale (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 5:6).

fine and found fine, even though they are not the finest, than which there is none higher, etc.. When they agreed on fine wheat and the wheat sold is not the finest but still falls under the definition of fine wheat, even if there is a difference of a sixth between the usual price and the price paid, the buyer cannot retract from the sale but only ask for the return of the difference in price (as in the law of overcharge by a sixth, see above 12:2). In the same way, if they agreed on poor wheat and the wheat sold is not the poorest but still falls under the definition of poor wheat, the seller cannot retract (and if he received a sixth less than what was due to him, he may demand this from the buyer).
reddish. Of a reddish hue.
can retract from his fellow. He may back out of the transaction with his fellow, even if his fellow wants to uphold it.

for this is not the kind that he said he would sell him. Rather it is a different kind, and there is no side that loses, since some people prefer wine and some prefer vinegar (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 5:6).

even if he said to him: I need it for a cooked dish. Even if the buyer said that he does not want to drink it all at once but to keep it for prolonged use in seasoning dishes, the seller is not liable for it, since the souring may have been caused by pouring the wine into jars or by a defect in the buyer's jars.

and if he knew that his wine turns sour, it is a mistaken purchase. If the buyer asked for wine for a dish, and the seller gave him wine that tends to sour quickly, it is a mistaken purchase, since it is not suited for a dish (Maggid Mishneh).
I need it for a stew. For the purpose of a cooked dish.
here is your wine and your jars. Return my money and take the wine and the jars.
within the first three days, it is at the seller's risk. If the wine soured within three days of the sale, it was apparently defective from the start, and the seller must bear responsibility.

one who sells a barrel of wine to his fellow in order to sell it little by little. The buyer specified that he needs wine that keeps for a long time, because he intends to sell it little by little, and this refers to wine that is in the seller's barrel.
and it soured in its half or in its third. The wine soured in half or a third of the barrel.
it returns to the seller. As in the law of one who says 'I need it for a stew' (above, halachah 3).
and if the buyer changed its tap hole. He made a tap for it in a different place.

it is at the buyer's risk. He cannot return it to the seller, because moving the barrel in order to make a tap could hasten the souring, and also if he delayed in selling the wine, he caused himself the loss (Meiri, Bava Batra 98a).
one who receives a barrel of wine from his fellow, etc.. Reuven gave Shimon a barrel of wine, and they agreed that Shimon would sell the barrel elsewhere and they would divide the profits.

it is at the seller's risk, since the barrel and the wine are his. Reuven, the owner of the barrel, bears the loss, since Shimon's moving the barrel and delaying the sale were done in accordance with their agreement (Meiri, Bava Batra 98a).
spiced wine. Prepared and improved.

he must make it last for him until Shavuot. The seller is responsible that the wine will keep until the festival of Shavuot, but after that he is not responsible, since the heat of the Tammuz season spoils even fine wine.
aged three years. Wine produced in the year before last, which together with the current year has existed for three years.

and it must last and not turn sour until the festival. Aged wine is wine that ages and keeps for three full years, and therefore it is the seller's responsibility until the end of the current year at the festival of Sukkot, which is the time of the grape harvest (Rashbam, Bava Batra 98a-b).

this cellar of wine I sell you for a stew. When the seller says to the buyer 'this cellar,' the buyer accepts the contents of the cellar as they are, even if the quality of part of the wine is not good. On the other hand, the seller specified that the wine is good for a stew, and on that basis the buyer expects wine that lasts for some time (Kesef Mishneh).
or he sold him a cellar of wine without specification. He did not say 'this cellar,' and on the other hand did not specify that the wine is good for a stew.
more than this he need not accept. If the inferior jars are found to be more than a tenth of the whole transaction, it is a mistaken purchase.
he said to him: I sell you a cellar of wine for a stew. They agreed upon a cellar of good wine for a cooked dish.
or he said to him: I sell you a barrel of wine. Even though he did not say 'for a stew,' for in a single barrel the buyer does not accept that part of the wine be slightly sour.

he said to him: this cellar of wine, he gives him the wine sold in a shop. In this case he bought the contents of the cellar, provided it is of average quality, fit to be called 'wine' (see Bavli Bava Batra 95b).
this cellar I sell you. They agreed upon the contents of the cellar as they are.
even if it is all vinegar, it is his. The buyer cannot retract.
a trough. A large bowl.
a piece of wood from which a trough can be hollowed. A block of wood that can be carved and made into a trough.
to deceive them. To mislead them.

to deceive people with words. By speech alone, even if not in commercial matters, such as causing another to think that one wants to do a certain thing for him when in fact this is not true (see Hilchot De'ot 2:6).
one may not adorn. One may not embellish.
a person. One who is being sold as a slave (for example, dyeing his white beard so that he will look young; Bavli Bava Metzia 60b).
but one may polish new ones. Since he only cleans and beautifies them, and does not cause deception.
he shall rub. He shall scrub.

one may not daub a person with the water of chizrim. One may not smear on him water of a kind of thorns called 'chizrim,' which because of their sharpness cause a swollen appearance (lexicon of R. Tanchum Yerushalmi, entry 'sharbet').
nor may one color the face with sarak. With red coloring.
nor may one inflate the innards. It is forbidden to inflate the intestines of an animal so that it will look large.
nor may one soak the meat in water. So that its color will change and it will look choice (Rashi, Bava Metzia 60b), or in order to increase its weight (Rabbenu Baruch the Spaniard, ibid.).

nor may one sell the meat of a carcass to a gentile as part of the meat of a properly slaughtered animal. When a gentile buys slaughtered meat from a Jew, one may not give him carcass meat without his knowledge, even if one lowers the price for him on that account, since the gentile will think that he was given expensive meat at a cheap price and will be needlessly grateful (see also Hilchot De'ot 2:6).
to sort the groats. To remove the waste mixed in the beans ground in a mill.
but not from the mouth of the storage bin. One may not sort only the beans found at the opening of the container in which they are stored.
and he lowers below the market price in order to increase those who buy from him on credit. He reduces from the accepted price in order to attract buyers who will buy from him on credit.
one may not mix fruits with fruits. If a person sells fruits from a certain place, he may not mix other fruits into them.
even if the old ones are expensive and the new ones cheap. And he sells everything at the cheap price.
because the buyer wishes to store them. To keep them for some time, and the old ones are liable to rot.

with wine they permitted mixing strong with weak only at the winepresses. To mix strong wine with weak wine while they are new and have not yet fermented sufficiently, since they ferment together and the different flavors blend well.
he may not sell it in a shop unless he informs him. He informs the buyers that the wine is diluted.
to the merchant. A trader.

lest he deceive others with it. The merchant buys in order to sell to others, and he may not bother to inform them; in particular, the merchant might permit himself not to inform, because he did not see the mixing of water (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 228:21).
and this applies only if it is at the winepresses. During fermentation, when the water blends well into it (Maggid Mishneh).
the merchant takes from five, etc.. Since everyone knows that they did not grow in his own fields but that he took them from various people.
a pitas. A large jar.
a storage bin. A storehouse (a warehouse or large vessel).
provided that he does not intend to mix. That he does not intend to deceive by mixing bad with good and the like.
it is forbidden to mix lees. One may not mix different lees, since the lees of one barrel could spoil another barrel.

and even lees of last night with lees of the day is forbidden. Even the lees left in the barrel from yesterday's wine may not be mixed with today's wine, though it is placed into the same barrel (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 228:10).
he puts his lees into it. For every wine has lees, and its own lees do not harm it.
he does not accept lees. If they agreed on a certain quantity of refined oil, the seller must give him this quantity without any admixture of lees at all.
he accepts one and a half logs of lees per hundred logs. If the oil contains this amount of lees, the buyer must accept it.
and with the other lees he accepts cloudy oil, etc.. Besides the lees, the buyer accepts upon himself cloudy oil that floats on top of the oil.

in addition to the lees known in that place. The floating oil is in addition to the lees in the amount stated above (a log and a half of lees per hundred logs). This amount is determined according to the custom at the time and place of the sale (see below, halachah 12).
when does this apply. That the buyer must accept the cloudy oil in addition to the lees.

and he bought the oil in Nisan by the measure of Tishrei, which is larger, etc.. In Tishrei sellers customarily measure oil in a larger vessel, because at the time of the olive harvest part of the oil is still cloudy and floats on top of the rest of the oil, and the buyer does not benefit from it. But in Nisan the oil is clear and is measured in a smaller vessel. Therefore, a person who paid in Tishrei and takes clear oil in Nisan, if he wants the seller to measure for him in the Tishrei vessel according to the time he paid, must accept upon himself the cloudy oil, that is, the seller deducts from the quantity of oil the amount of cloudy oil that floated on top in Tishrei (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 228:28).

one who sells wheat to his fellow accepts a quarter of kitonot per se'ah. If the buyer finds a quarter of a kav of legumes in six kavs (a se'ah) of wheat, he must accept this as natural, since legumes grow in wheat fields (in seasons when wheat is not grown) and tend to get mixed into sacks of wheat.
nishovot. Straw, or chaff that comes from the ears of grain (Rashbam, Bava Batra 94a); or it means barley that dried out in the wind and was emptied of its kernels (Yad Ramah, ibid.).
dust. Earth.
wormy. Infested with worms.
filth. Dirt.
he must sift all of it. The buyer returns the goods to the seller, and the seller must sift all of it.
one who picks out a pebble from his fellow's grain pile. One who removes a stone or dirt from his fellow's grain, where what he removed was not more than the accepted amount of waste in that place.
according to the size of the pebble he picked out. By the measure of the volume of the pebble he removed.
if it was sold by the measure of the wheat. If he were selling everything, he would receive payment for that pebble as well.
and if you say he should return it. If you ask why he should not put the pebble back into the grain.

they have said that it is forbidden to mix even a little. Although it is permitted to sell grain into which a little waste has become mixed, to mix waste in deliberately is forbidden even in a small amount (see Yerushalmi Kil'ayim 2:1).
jars. Clay vessels.

pitasot. Defective jars, whose firing process that makes them fit for use was not completed (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 6:2; it may be a different word from the 'pitas' mentioned above, halachah 7).
fine and made with sulfur. That they were placed in the fumes of burning sulfur, to add beauty to them, strengthen the clay, and seal pores and cracks.
claimants. Those who dispute ownership.
for even though the responsibility is upon him. To return to the buyer the money he paid if the purchase is taken from him, as below, halachah 3.

a person does not want to give his money, etc.. A person does not want to pay for something that will cause him to need a court, even if he knows he will not lose his money, and this is like selling an item with a defect (which must be disclosed to the buyer, as above, 18:1).
in one of the ways by which one acquires. By money, by a document, or by chazakah (above, 1:3).
claimants came forward against it. For example, they claim that the seller robbed it from them.
and let him litigate with the claimants. The seller will stand against them in court.
and if the buyer made any use of it. Use for enjoyment after claimants came forward against it.
he trampled its boundary and merged it with the land. He lowered the boundary that was between the field and the adjacent field, until they appear as one.
he cannot retract. Since after using it he waived the defect (as above, 15:3).

rather he litigates with the claimants. Even though the seller is responsible for the land, he can nonetheless say to the buyer, 'If they take it from you through court, I will return your money' (Bavli Bava Metzia 14b).
like the law of all those who lose through seizure. Like the law of a buyer who lost the purchase to the seller's creditors.
even if he sold the land by a document. In which it is customary to write all the terms of the sale.
for the omitted guarantee is a scribe's error. It must be assumed that the scribe erred or forgot to mention it, because a person does not pay without being sure of the return he receives.
a creditor of the seller came and seized it from the buyer. He took the field in payment of his debt.
whether by royal law or by their courts. By decree of the king or in a gentile court.

the seller owes nothing. Although money was taken from him according to their law, there is no proof that this is the truth, and it may be that money was taken unlawfully. For their rules of evidence differ from Jewish law, and their witnesses may lie and the like (Or Sameach).
an earthquake. A trembling of the earth.
the unusual. Something uncommon.

and the river in which they used to transport goods was cut off. A dam was made that stops the passage of boats in a river regularly used for transporting merchandise (see Bavli Gittin 73a and Rashi there).
and it left the buyer's hand. The owner of the land, who was robbed by the seller, took his land out of the buyer's hand.
the seller owes nothing. For the seller can claim that he sold it to him without guarantee, so that he would not come back at him with claims in any case (Bavli Bava Batra 44b).
needless to say if a creditor came and seized it. In this case the buyer cannot claim, 'You sold me something that is not yours.'
and Levi came to take it out of Shimon's hand. For example, he claims that Reuven robbed it from him.
if Reuven wished to litigate with Levi. To stand against Levi in court in place of Shimon.
what have I to do with you, for you have no responsibility. You are not a party to my case, for you sold the field without guarantee and you will not lose if I take it from the buyer.

he cannot go back against Shimon, etc.. When land is taken from a person who bought with a guarantee, he claims the price of the land from the seller, and if the seller himself bought the land with a guarantee, he claims the money from the one who sold to him. In this case, when Reuven's creditor seized the field from Reuven, one might have said that Reuven could claim from Shimon (for he bought the field from him with a guarantee), while Shimon could not claim back from Reuven (for he bought from him without a guarantee). But the law is that Reuven did not accept responsibility in the case of other people taking the land or the price of the land from Shimon, but he certainly accepted responsibility in the case where he himself claims from Shimon the price of land seized because of a debt that he himself owes, and therefore Shimon can claim it back from him.
Yaakov, their father. Reuven's father, who bequeathed the field to him (Maggid Mishneh).
he goes back against Shimon for the full price. Reuven claims the price of the land from Shimon, and Shimon cannot claim it back from him.

and Reuven did not accept upon himself for Shimon the responsibility of others at all. Reuven did not take upon himself responsibility in the case that another person takes from Shimon (such as a creditor of Reuven), nor did he take upon himself responsibility in the case that he himself takes from Shimon because the land was seized by a creditor of another person, and even Reuven's father is considered another person for this purpose.
for a maneh. One hundred zuz, half the sum the seller proposed.
and he took the article without specification. Without their discussing the price.
if the seller was the one who demanded of the buyer and gave him the article. The seller was the one who initiated the giving of the article.
he gives only a maneh. Since the seller wanted to complete the sale, it must be assumed that he agreed to sell at the price the buyer stated (compare Hilchot Ishut 7:19).

he places the price of the purchase between them and withdraws. He places the price of the purchase in the court and withdraws himself from the case (Maggid Mishneh; for a similar law regarding a deposit see Hilchot Sheelah U'Pikadon 5:4).
or until Elijah comes. And clarifies the doubt, if they do not admit on their own.
and if he was pious. One who acts beyond the letter of the law.
and denied it and swore falsely. The seller demanded that he pay, and he claimed that he had paid.
and he says: I do not know. He does not know whom he denied, although at first he knew from whom he had bought.
because he committed a transgression. And the Sages penalized him, like the law of one who robs one of five people and does not know from whom (see Hilchot Gezelah 4:9).
the owner of the merchandise. The seller.
when the merchandise comes out from under his hand. When the item sold is still in the seller's hand.
but if the merchandise does not come out from under his hand. Rather both hold it and each claims that it was sold to him.
he is only one witness. Whose testimony obligates only an oath (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:1).

and his law regarding this testimony is like that of any person, for he has no interest in his testimony. For he has already received his money and has no benefit from the testimony, and therefore he is not an interested party, which would disqualify him from testifying (see Hilchot Edut 15:1).

and he took from one with his consent and from one against his will. One buyer paid with the seller's consent, and another buyer paid without his consent after he had already agreed to sell to the first.
there is no testimony here at all. For the seller does not know.

he swears by the Sages' enactment. An oath that the Sages instituted when two people hold an article and each claims it is his, so that each will not seize his fellow's article (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 9:7).
while holding an object. While the one swearing holds a Torah scroll in his hand (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
and half the price. For both of them paid for all of it.
there was no proof there. The one seeking to take did not bring witnesses who prove his claim.
a heset oath. An oath that the Sages instituted for one who denies a claim (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).

he swears a Torah oath like all the other claims. See Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:1. This oath is more stringent than the heset oath, as it is taken while holding an object, with the one swearing holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:13).
and the householder. The buyer.

since they have already left the seller's possession, etc.. Since the fruits are lying in the public domain, neither the buyer nor the seller is in possession of them. But since the seller admits that he gave the fruits to the buyer, the buyer's claim regarding the fruits has the advantage, and he may take them after swearing while holding an object (see above, halachah 4) that he paid the seller (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 7:6 and the commentary of the Rif, Shevuot 31a-b in the Rif's pages).

and if they were in the buyer's possession, he would swear a heset oath and be exempt. If they were in the buyer's possession, he would be the one in possession, and he would be exempt by the lighter heset oath rather than the oath by the Sages' enactment.

and if they were still in the shopkeeper's possession, he would swear a heset oath. If the fruits were still in the seller's possession, he would be the one in possession of the fruits, and he would be exempt by a heset oath that he did not receive the dinar.

for he never admitted to him that he sold them. In this case the seller's claim regarding the fruits is stronger than the buyer's, since both parties agree that the fruits were not yet given to the buyer, and therefore the shopkeeper swears while holding an object on his claim and takes the fruits (see the commentary of the Rif, Shevuot 31b in the Rif's pages).
like one who gives a dinar to a money changer to receive coins. A person who gives a dinar to a money changer in order to receive coins from him.

one who exchanges a cow for a donkey and it gave birth, and likewise one who sells his maidservant and she gave birth. In these cases the cow or the maidservant were acquired at the time the act of acquisition was performed, wherever they were, without performing an act on their bodies (above, 2:1, 5:1). Since they are not before them at the time of the transfer, a dispute may arise between the parties whether they gave birth before the act of acquisition, in which case the offspring belongs to the seller, or after the act of acquisition, in which case the offspring belongs to the buyer.
even if the seller said I do not know, the buyer must bring proof. Because the seller was their previous owner, it is decided that they gave birth while in his ownership until proven otherwise.
even though the cow is standing in a swamp and the maidservant is standing in an alley. Places that belong to no one, in which the seller has no presumption of possession on account of the place.

they are in the seller's presumptive possession until the buyer brings proof. For the buyer claims that they gave birth when they were his, and if he can prove this, he will take the offspring out of the seller's possession. As long as this is not proven, even though the seller does not know, the offspring should be left in the presumptive possession of the previous owner.

the seller shall swear while holding an object regarding the cow's offspring. He swears that the cow gave birth while it was still his. And if he claims that he does not know, he swears that he does not know (as below, halachah 13).
as will be explained in Hilchot To'en VeNit'an. 5:1.
this one says: I do not know. When she gave birth, and perhaps she gave birth when she was in my possession.

and it is not in the possession of either of them, they divide. If the cow or maidservant is in a domain that belongs to neither of them, they divide the value of the offspring between them. Although the previous halachah says that the buyer must bring proof even when the seller said 'I do not know,' that is because the buyer made a definite claim and therefore the burden of proof is upon him, and if he does not bring it, the situation is left in the presumptive possession of the previous owner. But in the case discussed here, where the buyer also does not know, the situation is balanced, and the presumption of the previous owner does not by itself have the force to make the buyer lose (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 223:2; see Maggid Mishneh and Sma there, subsection 2, who reconciled the two halachot in other ways).
the claimant wins the offspring. For the other's silence is considered an admission.
anyone in whose possession the doubt arose. Where a doubt became known and emerged regarding an item in his possession.

one who exchanges a cow for a donkey and the owner of the donkey pulled the cow. By this pulling the acquisition was completed, so that the cow is acquired by the owner of the donkey and the donkey is acquired by the owner of the cow (above, 5:1).
and the owner of the cow did not manage to pull the donkey before the donkey died. The donkey was found dead before the owner of the cow managed to take it from the owner of the donkey.

the owner of the donkey must bring proof, etc.. Since the donkey died in his possession. And if he has no proof he must return the cow, for if the donkey died before the cow was pulled, it is a mistaken purchase, since the owner of the cow did not intend to transfer his cow in exchange for a dead donkey.

a needle found in the thickness of the beit hakosot, etc.. The beit hakosot is one of the compartments of the stomach of a ruminant, and the thickness of the beit hakosot is where there is a double layer of skin. When a needle is found in the thickness of the beit hakosot after slaughter, the animal is considered a treifah only if two conditions combine: that the needle pierced the entire thickness of the wall (a 'through puncture'), and that a little blood ('a drop of blood') was found on the needle, which proves that the needle was there before slaughter (Hilchot Shechitah 6:12). The halachah here speaks of a butcher who bought an animal and after slaughter found a needle in such a way that the animal is considered a treifah, and he claims that it became a treifah in the seller's possession and so it is a mistaken purchase.
if the mouth of the wound had healed. If a thin skin had formed over it.

it is known that it was a treifah three days before the slaughter. For the wound had already healed, and if the buyer slaughtered within three days of the purchase, it was certainly a treifah before that, and so it is a mistaken purchase.
he pays the price to the seller. He pays him the price of a kosher animal.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 14, that the burden of proof lies on the one in whose possession the doubt arose.
something unspecified. That is not defined (see also Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 3:5).
that he found less or more than the estimate they had in mind. The buyer discovered that the quantity is less than he thought, or the seller discovered that the quantity is greater than he thought.
and they have overreaching according to the market price. If the price does not match the accepted price, the laws of overreaching explained in chapter 12 apply.
as we have explained. Above, 13:2, that the laws of overreaching also apply to a sale that is not measured.
for the buyer's mind was not made up. The buyer had not firmly decided to buy.
and this is nothing but like one playing with a kuvya. He does not intend to buy seriously, but in jest and mockery (Mea'rak).

he gives him according to the market price at the time of the sale. He gives him a quantity of wheat whose market price is ten dinars at the time the buyer paid (even if in the meantime the price of wheat has changed).
he accepts the curse 'He who punished'. As we have explained, above, 7:1-2, regarding one who retracts from a purchase after payment.
one who sells a place to his fellow to build a house on it, etc.. He sold him an area so that the buyer would build on it a house or a stable.
one who contracts with his fellow to make for him, etc.. A contractor who undertook to build for his fellow.
a house for a wedding for his son. For him to live in after his marriage.
a house for widowhood for his daughter. For her to live in after she is widowed.
he makes four cubits by six. These are the minimum dimensions for a dwelling for a person or for cattle.
he sold him the place of a large house. For he stated so in the sale.
he sold him the place of a banquet hall. A spacious hall.
the garden courtyard. A courtyard made for ornament.
and the height of each house is half its length and half its width. The height of each of these structures must be half its length plus half its width.
the measure of the cave is four cubits by six. This is the area of the central space of the cave from which the burial niches extend.
six handbreadths. A cubit.

so between each grave on the sides there is a cubit and a half. The total width of the graves is three cubits, so the total space between them is three cubits, and between each grave there is a cubit and a half of space.
one who sells his fellow, within his field, a place for a water channel. A certain place within the seller's field for a water channel for the buyer.
a beit shelachin. A field that needs constant irrigation (Hilchot Shemittah VeYovel 1:8).
to its banks. To its raised sides.
a water channel for watering with a pail. A small channel from which one draws with a bucket to water animals, wash clothes, and the like.

the field owner may plant them but may not sow them, for seeds loosen the soil. The roots of a planting go deep into the ground, whereas the roots of seeds spread sideways near the surface and weaken the soil.
if its banks crumbled. Disintegrated.
for on this condition, etc.. That if the banks are ruined, the owner of the channel will take earth from the seller's field.
if he sold him a path for an individual. For the passage of one person.

he gives him a width of eight cubits along the length of the path. A width of eight cubits along the entire length of the path. This width allows two wagons coming opposite each other to pass (Rashbam, Bava Batra 100a).
he gives him a width of sixteen cubits. See also Hilchot Shabbat 14:1, Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 3:3, Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 13:27.
the king's road. Which he makes for his war (Hilchot Melachim 5:3).
and the burial road. Which is made for a funeral.
it has no measure. For the width of the road varies according to their needs.
for this is like selling something whose kind is not known. That he did not acquire, as above, halachah 1.
he sold him a place for a standing area. A place where people stand to eulogize the dead or to comfort mourners.
a beit arba'at kavin. An area for sowing four kavs.

and he gave him one boundary long and one boundary short. The seller specified the boundary of the field so that one side is longer than the opposite side, for example the west side longer than the east side.
if the long one belonged to one person. It borders the field of one person.

he acquired of the long one only opposite the short one. The buyer receives a rectangular area opposite the short side only, for it must be assumed that the seller did not intend the stated boundaries to define the area precisely, but only as a general identification of the property, like one who says to his fellow, 'I sell you the area between Reuven's house and Shimon's house.'

and if it belonged to two, he acquires up to the line of the end. If part of the long boundary borders the property of one person and part borders the property of another, and nevertheless the seller stated the entire length of the boundary, this proves that the seller meant to state precise boundaries, and therefore the buyer receives the entire area between the long boundary and the short boundary, by drawing a diagonal line ('rosh tor') from the end of the long boundary to the end of the short boundary.
if Reuven's boundary was east and west. Reuven has a field to the east of the field sold, and another field to the west.

he must write him 'Reuven's boundary on two sides,' etc.. In order for the buyer to receive the entire rectangular area between Reuven's fields and Shimon's fields, he must write that he sells him the area between Reuven's boundary on two sides and Shimon's boundary on two sides. But if he wrote that he sells him the area between Reuven and Shimon, the buyer receives only half of the field, like a triangle one side of which is one of Reuven's fields (for example the eastern field), the second side is one of Shimon's fields (for example the southern field), and the third side cuts the rectangle diagonally (Rashbam, Bava Batra 62a; see the diagram).
he gave him the first boundary, etc.. He sold his fellow a field and specified boundaries for him on only three sides.
but the fourth boundary. The furrow on which the boundary itself lies, which is sometimes recognizable and distinct from the rest of the field.
if it was swallowed up within the boundaries. It is within the boundaries of the other boundaries.
a row of date palms. A line of palms.
and it does not contain nine kavs. An area in which nine kavs can be sown may be called a field (see Hilchot Shecheinim 1:4), and so it is considered independent.
he acquired the fourth boundary also. For it has no independent significance, and it must be assumed that it was included in the sale.

if it was swallowed up and has on it, etc.. When the fourth boundary is swallowed up, but on the other hand has significance because of the row of date palms on it or the nine-kav sowing area in it. Or the opposite: that it is distinct by itself because it is not swallowed up, but on the other hand has no row of date palms or nine kavs.
the matter is entrusted to the court, etc.. They will assess the seller's intent.

he specified for him only the corner and did not specify the boundary of the whole side. He defined and stated only the points at the corners of the field, and did not define the entire length of the boundaries.
or he specified for him two boundaries in the shape of a gimmel. He defined the boundaries on only two sides adjacent to each other, like the Greek letter gamma, whose shape is Γ.
or he specified for him part by part on every side. He stated the boundaries on all sides, but on each side stated only parts of it alternately, like a dotted line.

he acquires of it as much as he gave him, and as the judges see fit. The buyer receives the area adjacent to what the seller stated, and regarding the rest of the field the matter depends on the discretion of the judges, since there is doubt whether he intended to sell the whole field or only the area he stated (see Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh).
one who sells his fellow a house in a large birah. A house located within a large building.
he gave him the outer boundaries. The seller specified the outer boundaries of the entire birah.
for it was the boundaries that he broadened for him. The seller specified wide, imprecise boundaries, because his intent was only a general identification of the location of the property.
and I did not leave for myself. I did not leave for myself.
even three and four. He must give him all the fields he has.
he said to him: my properties, even gardens and orchards. For the word 'properties' means real estate.
he shows him the one who died or the one that fell. And says to him, 'Here is yours before you.'
for the hand of the holder of the document is on the bottom. Because he comes to take from the one in possession, as in any monetary doubt.
the field of Devei Chayyei. In other versions: 'the field of Devei Chiyya,' and so it appears in our text of the Gemara (Bavli Bava Batra 61b).
it is called so, and it never was his. People call it 'Reuven's field' although it never was his.
rather this is the one that was, etc.. I bought another field from Reuven, and that is the one I intended to sell you.
the simple name in everyone's mouth. The accepted and common name.
I sell you half my field. And he did not specify which half.
they appraise. They assess.
from the poorest part of it. From the inferior part of the field, because the seller has the upper hand and prefers the best part of it.
that which is worth half the price of the whole field. An area equal in value to half the field.
and he gives him in its south half the whole price. An area on the south side equal in value to half the field.
to make in his portion the place of the fence. For the purpose of separation between the two parcels.
lest the weasel jump. Over the fence and cause damage.
he had half a field. He was a partner with another person in the field.
he said to him: half of the field that I have. Half of my portion in the field.
he said to him: the boundary of the field from which it is divided. He stated the boundary from which onward the field is divided, and from this boundary onward he does not transfer to him.
if he said to him: and these are its boundaries. If he stated all the boundaries of the field.
he acquired half of it. The entire half of the field, from the boundary from which the field is divided to the outer boundaries he marked for him.
and if he did not give him its boundaries. Rather he stated only the boundary from which it is divided.

he acquired only a beit tish'at kavin. An area in which nine kavs are sown, which is the minimum area called a field (Hilchot Shecheinim 1:4), and no more than that, because the seller did not state the other boundaries, and it must be assumed that he intended to sell only a small area of no great significance.

something that has not yet come into the world. Something that does not exist in reality at present but will exist in the future (but one may transfer the substance of the thing for its fruits even though the fruits do not yet exist, as below, 23:1).
with the gift of a person on his deathbed. A dangerously ill person about to die, whose gift has great validity (see Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 8:2).
one who sells the fruits of a date palm to his fellow. Before they grew.
he can retract even after the fruits have come into the world. Because the sale is not valid.
and if the buyer shook them down. He took the fruits down from the tree.
they are not taken out of his hand. It must be assumed that the seller waived his claim, for the seller agreed to this transaction even though he erred in the law (Rashi, Bava Metzia 66b).

he is not obligated to accept the curse 'He who punished'. Unlike one who retracts after payment (see above, 7:1), because the sale of something that has not come into the world has no validity at all.

but one who stipulates on the market price, etc.. A buyer who paid the seller for certain goods according to the market price at that hour, where these goods are not now in the seller's possession but in the hands of other merchants in the market.

the seller is obligated to buy and give... and if he retracted, etc.. For the payment the buyer paid has validity as in any sale, since the goods are available in the market and are considered something that has come into the world.
one who stipulated on the market price... if they were ears of grain. A buyer who paid at the market price for grain not yet harvested.
he has acquired, so as to receive the curse 'He who punished'. The payment has significance in that the one who retracts receives 'He who punished,' as in any sale.
and this applies only if he is seen at the threshing floor. That the buyer comes to the threshing floor to show the seller that he is serious about buying from him.
or he says to him in the market: I am relying on you. That the buyer informs the seller that he relies on his goods and intends to buy from him and not from another.
the seller's mind was not made up. He is not sure that the buyer will buy from him, and therefore he too does not commit himself to the transaction.

for he says, etc.. The seller says in his heart that perhaps the buyer made an arrangement with another seller; since the grain has not yet been harvested and it is not known whether it is good, the buyer prefers to arrange with additional sellers in order to be sure he will have good grain (Bavli Bava Metzia 63b and commentators there).

he does not transfer it, and it is like something that has not come into the world. It is treated like something that has not come into the world, which the seller cannot transfer (and see further in the Rulings and Opinions).
his sale is a valid sale because of his livelihood. The Sages enacted that the sale stands for the sake of the livelihood essential for his existence.
and the property was found in the father's possession. The property still belongs to his father's father, since the sale is not valid (see Rulings and Opinions).

and he gave him on top of it a hundred dinars. He transferred to him along with the land a hundred dinars by the method of 'agav,' for instance where the giver said to the recipient, 'Acquire the dinars along with the land' (see above, 3:8-9).
and if he has no dinars. If the giver claims that he did not have dinars in his possession at the time of the gift.
one who had a deposit in the hand of another. Which he left with his fellow to guard.
and if the one with whom it was deposited denied it. He claimed that he did not receive it or that he returned it.

since it was given for spending, it is not in the world. Since the borrower uses the coins he received and will return other coins to the lender, the coins he will return are not considered to be in the lender's possession.
and it is a matter that has no reason. The method of transfer is not understandable, and it is like a decree.
as we have explained. Above, 6:8.
he transfers the document by writing and delivery. He writes to him 'Acquire such-and-such document and every lien in it' and hands him the document (above, 6:11).
since a person's mind is close to his son. And he certainly made up his mind to transfer it to him.
'acquire like this animal or like this fetus' he has acquired nothing. Because he made his fellow's acquisition depend on the acquisition of the animal or fetus.
a person does not transfer, etc.. See also Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 10:15.
the color of crystal. The color of the crystal stone.
residence in this house. Living in this house.
as will be explained. Below, 23:1-2.
he is obligated to fulfill his word. When his animal gives birth.

the poor acquired them. For the heirs are obligated to fulfill the dead man's words and give to the poor, just as he himself would have been obligated to do so had he been alive (Maggid Mishneh; and see Kesef Mishneh and Merkeves HaMishneh, Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 6:33, who explained in other ways).

and my mind does not incline to these words, etc.. Rambam disagrees with these Geonim, and holds that one should not equate a poor person with any other person, for a person is not commanded to transfer his property to another person, but he is commanded to fulfill his words regarding charity, and by virtue of this the poor acquire even something that has not come into the world.
as we have explained in Arachin. Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 6:31-32.

a person may transfer the substance for its fruits. A person who wants to transfer to his fellow the future produce of a certain asset may transfer to him the substance of the asset with regard to its fruits, and in this way he is not considered to be transferring something that has not come into the world (above, 22:1).

to what is this similar? To one who rents a house, etc.. Selling the substance for its fruits is similar to renting a house or field, where he also does not sell the substance of the thing but the right to benefit from it by using it or its fruits (and see below, halachah 8, the difference between these two acquisitions).

one who sold his slave for the fine, etc.. He sold the slave only with regard to the right to receive the fine in the case where the slave is killed by a forewarned ox that gored him, in which the owner of the ox must pay thirty shekels to the owner of the slave (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 11:1).
it is a doubt. For this case differs from fruits that come out of a tree by themselves, since the fine does not come from the slave's body, or since it is not certain that there will be a fine.
therefore he did not acquire, etc.. By the law of monetary doubt (see above, 3:1).
one who sold a tree to one and its fruits to another. He transferred the tree to one person and the fruits to another person.

he did not reserve the place of the fruits, and the other has nothing. It must be assumed that the seller sold the first buyer the entire body of the tree and did not leave for the second the place where the fruits grow, so that the second acquired fruits that have not yet come into the world and receives nothing, and the fruits that will grow belong to the first buyer.
regarding himself he reserves with a generous eye. And therefore he surely kept for himself also the place where the fruits grow, and the buyer has only the trunk when it dries.
one who sells the substance of land for a fixed time. A complete sale including substance and fruits for all purposes, except that they set a certain date on which the sale expires.
one who sells this field for its fruits. That he acquired also the fruits that will grow in it.
one who sells the fruits of this field to his fellow, he has not acquired. Because one cannot transfer something that has not come into the world.
as we have explained. Above, 22:1-2.

the buyer may not use this field at all... except at the time of taking out the fruits. He has no right at all in the field, and even if he had acquired the fruits, he would not be permitted to enter the field except at the time of taking them out.
and the field owner may. The field owner is permitted.

and the buyer may use it as he wishes. He may use the substance of the land as he wishes, such as agricultural work as in the next halachah, but he may not change the form of the land as in the previous halachah.
or to leave it fallow. To leave it uncultivated and unworked.

but the renter is not so, as will be explained in the matter of hiring. The renter may not deviate from what is customary or from what the landlord stipulated with him, as explained in Hilchot Sechirut, chapter 8.
and the renter may not sublet. To others, because he is not the owner (see Hilchot Sechirut 1:4).
and whoever buys may transfer to others all that he bought. A person who bought a certain thing, such as a field for its fruits, may transfer to another all his rights.
he acquired, and this is not selling something that has not come into the world. Even if he did not say explicitly that he is selling the dovecote or the beehive for their produce.

rather he sells the dovecote for its fruits and the beehive for its honey. It must be assumed that he intended to sell the substance of the dovecote and the beehive for the sake of the produce, since the intrinsic value of a dovecote and beehive is not great and they are secondary to the doves and the honey (Kesef Mishneh in his second explanation).
for he benefits from whatever is caught in it. The fish that will come into the channel.
and the law of all of them. Those who buy the substance of a thing for its fruits.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 1.

the owner of the dovecote does not acquire them as long as they have not flown. A person who owns a dovecote that belongs to him for all purposes does not acquire the eggs and fledglings born in the dovecote as long as they cannot fly, which is the time to which the commandment of sending away the mother bird applies (see Hilchot Shechitah 13:9).
and this matter is a decree of the Sages, etc.. See also Hilchot Shechitah 13:18.
and because of 'You shall not take the mother with the young' they touched it. Lest he take the mother while she is sitting on the fledglings or eggs.
he claps on the dovecote. He strikes with his hand.

until they fly and lift themselves off the ground. The fledglings fly a little, and since they have lifted themselves because of him, the owner of the dovecote acquires them through acquisition by lifting, and can transfer them to his fellow (see Ritva, Chullin 141b).
and afterward he may transfer them to his fellow by an act of acquisition. Kinyan sudar (above, 5:5).
or along with the land. Above, 3:8-9.
one who buys the produce of a dovecote from his fellow. He bought the dovecote for its fruits (as above, halachah 9).
because the mothers flee. The male and female founders of the dovecote flee because of loneliness.
and he has destroyed the dovecote. For the seller intended to sell only the squabs to be born, and not the dovecote itself.

and how many does he leave, etc.. It is the way of doves to give birth several times a year, a pair of squabs each time, usually a male and a female. And in order for the parent pair to remain in the dovecote, it needs two pairs of offspring who remain with it.
if there were mothers and daughters in it at the time of the sale of the fruits. If there was in the dovecote a parent pair and an offspring pair, which are not included in the sale.

he leaves the first brood that the mothers produce so that they may be accompanied, etc.. The buyer leaves for the seller the first pair that the parent pair produces, so that the parents have two pairs of offspring with them in the dovecote.

and from what the daughters produce he leaves two broods, etc.. He leaves for the seller two pairs that the offspring pair that were in the dovecote before the sale produce, in order to ensure that they remain in the dovecote.

he takes three swarms, etc.. In the summer, when the hive is full of honey, several swarms of thousands of bees each usually leave it. It is customary to take from the hive only three swarms a year, or a little more than three (in a case where many swarms emerge from it), and afterward one makes sure that bees remain in it in order to ensure the continued activity of the hive the following year.
he leaves in the hive two honeycombs. For the bees' sustenance in winter, which is the minimum required for their food until the honey supply is renewed in summer.
one who buys olive trees from his fellow to cut down. Olive trees, which the buyer cuts down in order to use their branches.
two cuttings. Shoots, branches that are planted.
a virgin sycamore. A wild fig that has not yet been cut.
a sycamore stump. One that has already been cut once and whose roots are strong.

from the knot upward. In the branch emerging from a vine, and likewise in a reed, there are knots containing buds for the renewal of the branch, and it is permitted to cut from the knot closest to where the branch emerges and upward (Meiri, Bava Kamma 81a).
he digs and uproots. He pulls out the root.
because its trunk does not renew. It does not grow again after being cut, and therefore there is no point in leaving any of the trunk.
one who sells three trees within his field. And did not specify that he is also selling the land with them.

three branches of trees. Three branches of three trees, where the trees are buried in the ground and the branches are visible (Einei David; and the Maggid Mishneh explained that it refers to three branches of one tree that are four cubits apart from each other and the earth covers the common trunk, so that they appear as three trees, and he wrote that the correct version is 'three branches of a tree').
the land fit for them. That they need.
and outside them the full space of the 'orah' and its basket. Around the trees, an area sufficient for the standing of a person picking figs (an 'orah') with his basket in hand.

neither of them may sow it except with the consent of his fellow. The buyer may not, because the area is encumbered to him only for picking, and the seller may not sow, lest the buyer's fruits that fall from the trees be soiled by the seeds.

standing like the three supports of a stove on which the pot is set. Planted like a tripod with three legs on which a pot is placed, that is, in a triangle, in which case it is difficult to work the area between them and it must be assumed that the field owner intended to sell it (Bavli Bava Batra 83b).

from four cubits up to sixteen cubits. For if there are less than four cubits between the trees they cannot develop, and if there are more than sixteen cubits they have no need for all the land between them.
and one on the boundary. On the boundary between the fields.

two within his own and another within his fellow's. The sale included two trees from the seller's area and one tree that is in the neighbor's area and belongs to the seller (for example, the seller bought it from the neighbor and now sells it to the buyer; Rashbam, Bava Batra 83a).
the public domain. That is, a road on which the public walks.
from the wide base of the trees. From the wide part of the trunk.
that he bought one after another. He bought them at different times.
a shoot. A branch emerging from the trunk.
the twigs. Thin branches.
and the tall branches. High branches.
for he has land. As above, halachah 2, and they grew in his land.

one who buys two trees within his fellow's field has no land. See Hilchot Bikkurim 4:4, where it is doubtful whether he has land or not, and here it is explained that in practice he has no land, because the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow.
lest they be drawn along the ground etc.. Lest one of the branches be drawn along the ground and become covered, and afterward sprout and appear as an additional tree.
all the wood that the owner of the two trees cuts from them. The small trees or branches that the owner of the two trees cuts from his trees.
that which sees the face of the sun. Whatever is exposed to view is considered trunk.
it belongs to the owner of the field. Because it is considered a growth of the ground, which belongs to the owner of the field.
because they have no trunk. Branches do not grow from the trunk; therefore everything that emerges from a date palm comes from its roots, even if it appears to emerge from the trunk.
as we have explained. Above, halachot 1-2.
brothers who divided. An inheritance.
an orchard. A planting of trees.
a white field. A grain field.
the owner of the orchard has four cubits inside the white field. For the needs of working the orchard.
and if it is a poor palm, all the more so the rest. If he specified a poor palm, it is to be understood from his words that all the more so he is keeping for himself the better palms.

he did not acquire any of the palms. The buyer does not receive even the palms that are poorer than the palm the seller specified (Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh), since it is to be assumed that the seller meant to exclude all the palms from the sale and did not bother to check which palm is the poorest, but specified one of the poor ones as an example (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 216:4; Aruch HaShulchan there, section 2).

if it has only palms, and he reserved the palms. Although palms are usually called by their own name and are not generally called simply 'trees'. But if there are other trees in the field, it is to be assumed that he meant to keep for himself those trees and not the palms (Bava Batra 69b).

if it had vines and palms, he reserved only the vines etc.. Because the term 'trees' fits vines better than palms (Rashbam there), and one cannot say that he meant to keep the palms for himself as well, since a person usually sells generously and gives the buyer a respectable portion.
and if he reserved the palms. Explicitly, or because the field had only palms.
and the rest belongs to the buyer. For a palm whose fruit can be picked without climbing has no importance, and it is included in the land.
he reserved from them only those that the yoke does not press down. He kept for himself the important trees that do not bend before the yoke of the plowing cow but obstruct the plowing.
one who says to his fellow, 'I am selling you land and palms'. They agreed that the seller would give the buyer land and also palms.

if he wished to buy him two palms, the sale is fulfilled. If the seller wants to buy two palms in order to sell them to the buyer, and give the buyer land with no palms on it plus the two palms he bought for him, the seller has fulfilled his commitment, since they agreed on land and palms and not on land that has palms on it.
'I am selling you land with palms'. Land that has palms on it.
he has no palms. The seller need not supply palms to the buyer.
and the branches. Boughs.

and although he acquired all of these even if he did not specify them, they are the adornment of the deed. Although the buyer receives the trees, the fruits and the branches even if the seller did not itemize them in the deed, nevertheless one should ideally itemize them, so that the deed will be fine and proper and no dispute will arise. [Note: Rambam writes and vocalizes the word 'noi' in his Commentary on the Mishnah as 'no'i'.]
and I have left nothing for myself in this sale. I have not kept anything in my possession.
and its height. Its elevation.

for the depth and the height are not acquired by default. One who sells a house and did not write 'and I have transferred to you its depth and its height' transferred only the house itself, without the right to build in the ground beneath it or in the air above it.

and since he transferred to him the depth and the height, he acquired the height etc.. If he wrote 'and I have transferred to you its depth and its height', he transferred to him the right to build in the ground and in the air, but did not transfer to him the structures already there.
and the dut. A pit whose walls are lined with stone.
and the gaps between the beams above. The channels between the stones and the plaster in the thickness of the roof.

on condition that the upper dyuta is mine. The story built on top of the house. Since in an unqualified sale it is his (for he did not transfer to the buyer the buildings above the house), the extra wording serves to give him additional rights (R. Yosef Migash and Rashbam, Bava Batra 63a-b).
and if he wished to put out projecting stones from it. To add stones to it that protrude outward, like shelves.
he builds as he did before. He may build on top of the dyuta just as he was permitted to before selling the house (Me'iras Einayim and others).
its standing place. The place where people stand to eulogize the dead or to comfort mourners.
members of the family come and bury there against his will. The seller's family buries him there against the buyer's will.
because of the disgrace to the family. An insult and disgrace to the family, who were accustomed to bury family members in one place set aside for them.
even though he did not specify. Even though the seller did not stipulate this at the time of sale.
one who sells something that has appurtenances. That has structures or fixtures that serve it.
he did not sell the yatziah around the house. The space between the walls of the house and an outer wall that surrounds the house.
