when the width of the yatziah was four cubits or more. So that it has importance of its own.
that opens into it by a skylight in the ceiling of the house. That one can ascend to the upper chamber through a window in the ceiling of the house.
he did not sell the room inside of it. An inner room whose use differs from the use of the house, such as a storeroom (Rashbam, Bava Batra 61a).

even though he gave him the outer boundaries. Even though the seller listed in the deed the houses that border the house on its various sides, we interpret that he meant only to define the location of the house and did not intend to transfer all the space between the houses he listed.
nor the dut built like a pit. A pit whose walls are lined with stone.
as we have explained. Above 24:15, that the sale of the depth and height does not include structures, unless he wrote to him 'from the ground of the abyss to the height of the heavens'.
for whoever sells, sells generously. And it is to be assumed that he did not keep for himself any part of the area he sold.

and if he said to him, 'I sold you the house except for the pit or the dut,' he need not acquire a path for him. This statement is superfluous wording, since the pit and the dut are not sold with the house even without this statement; therefore it is to be assumed that he meant by his words to keep the path for himself as well.
the buyer need not acquire a path for him. For it is to be assumed that the sale was made generously and includes a path as well.

they have no path through each other. For just as he sold generously to the inner one, so he sold generously to the outer one. The inner one must ask permission of the outer one or purchase a path to his house from him.
for whoever gives generously gives more than the seller. For by default he is giving a gift to his friend.
one who sells a house etc.. The basic rule in selling the appurtenances of a house is that anything fixed is sold as part of the house, and a movable item is not sold (Rashbam, Bava Batra 65a).
the frames of the doorways that are fixed in plaster. The beams fixed in the doorways of the house.
the bolt. A bar fixed in the wall.
the lock. The one fixed in the door.
the itzterovil. A millstone.
a kefifa. A basket.
the frames of the bed legs. Pieces of wood placed under the legs of the bed.
the frames of the windows. The frames of the windows.
trenches. Long, narrow excavations.
and all the outer houses. Those that open to the courtyard.
and the inner ones. Those that open to the outer houses.
and houses that have sand in them. Houses that are not paved but have sand on their floor, and are used for storage and the like (see Yad Ramah, Bava Batra 67a).
if they opened both this way and that way. To the courtyard and also to the outside.
if most of their use is within it. If the shops mainly serve the residents of the courtyard, because most of the customers are from the courtyard (Aruch HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 215:1).
he did not sell the bathhouse or the olive press in it. Because they have a name of their own and cannot be considered secondary to the courtyard (ibid.).
the cedar beams on which they lean at the time of pressing the olives. Posts on which they set the beam that presses the olives.
the vats. The place where the oil is collected.
these are the grinding stones. In which the olives are crushed and pounded before pressing.
the presses with which the olives are pressed. Wooden boards placed between the olives and the beam at the time of pressing.
the wheel. A kind of very large wooden screw, by means of which the beam is raised and lowered.
the sacks. Those made of wool, used for carrying olives.
the martzefin. Sacks made of leather.
if outside it there were shops in which olives or sesame are spread. Shops that, in addition to their regular use, also serve for spreading the produce of the olive press for drying before grinding.
the room of planks. A room in which one sits on wooden boards.
the room of the wooden cups from which water is taken. A room containing wooden cups in which water is brought for washing.
the room of the towels with which one dries oneself. A room in which one dries off with towels.
one who sells the city. A landed estate, like a large farm, in which all the fixed property found in it is the property of the owner of the estate.
and the irrigated fields in it. Fields that need watering.
and the woodlands designated for it. Woodlands set aside for the needs of the city.
and the fields known to belong to it. Fields that belong to the city.
and the animal, bird and fish preserves that face it. Fenced-in places for living creatures, whose openings face the city.
he did not sell its remnants. Portions of field that are separated from the main fields.
nor its daughters. Small estates attached to it.
nor the woodlands designated from it. Woodlands distant from the city.
nor the portion it has in the sea. When most of the city is on land and it has a small portion in the sea.
nor the portion it has on dry land. When most of the city is in the sea and only a minority of it is on land (Yad Ramah and Meiri, Bava Batra 68b).
if he sold the stones arranged for a fence. Stones arranged to support the fence (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 4:8).
and the stones placed on the sheaves. So that they will not be scattered by the wind.
because they are for its needs. These stones are permanently in the field for the sake of the field.
in order to support the vineyard. To lean the vine shoots on them.
that has reached the time of harvest. That has reached the end of its growth and is ready to be harvested.
a thicket of reeds. A group of reeds growing densely.
that is less than a beit rova. Whose area is less than the area for sowing a quarter-kav of grain.
the watchman's hut. The watchman's booth.
a carob tree that has not been grafted. A young carob tree that has not yet reached the stage of grafting, and therefore is secondary to the field.
a young sycamore. A young wild fig tree that has not yet been cut down.
and he sold all the palms in it. All the more so the other trees (Me'iras Einayim).
even though it is needed for the field. To lie in the field, dry out and air.
a bed of roses. A rose bed, a patch of roses.
nor the stump of a sycamore. A wild fig tree after it has been cut down, which is strong and valuable because its branches are used for beams, and therefore it is not secondary to the field.
and if he specified and said to him, 'except for these'. If the seller explicitly said that the sale of the field does not include the pit, or the winepress, or the dovecote.
he need not buy a path for himself. Because the explicit statement is superfluous, and it is to be assumed that he said it because he meant to keep a path for himself (see also above 25:3).

because the buyer could have specified and did not specify, he does not have these. It is the way of a buyer to inquire what is included in the sale in order to get the maximum value for the money he pays, and since he did not inquire, he has waived all the extras and receives only the minimum.

but one who gives a gift has acquired all of them etc.. A recipient of a gift is embarrassed to inquire what is included in it; therefore his silence is not considered a waiver, but we assume that the giver intends to give everything attached, except for what he explicitly says is not included (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 4:9).
and likewise brothers who divided. They divided among themselves their father's inheritance.

he acquired all of them. All the fixed items in the field. Some explain the reason is that brothers give to one another generously (Rabbeinu Gershom, Bava Batra 71a), and others explain that it is to be assumed that brothers want a complete division in which each receives his share and everything found in it (Tosafot there; see Hilchot Shecheinim 2:12).
one who takes possession of the property of a convert. A convert who died with no heirs, whose property is ownerless and whoever takes possession of it acquires it (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 1:6).
he consecrated all of them. For whoever consecrates, consecrates generously (Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 4:15).
they act as the Sages explained in these chapters. As detailed in chapters 24-28, according to the words of the Sages in the Mishnah and Gemara.
one who sells a ship etc.. The rule is that items fixed in the ship and serving its needs are sold along with it.
the mast. A wooden pole on which the sail is hung.
the sail. The sail.
the anchors. The anchor that holds the ship in one place.
the gangplank and the ladder. A bridge and a ladder.
the water room. A large vessel containing water.
the martzefin. Sacks into which merchandise is put.

he did not sell the mules that are not tied to it. He did not sell the wooden poles by which the wagon is pulled if they were separate from the wagon at the time of sale; and some explain that 'mules' are animals that pull the wagon (both explanations in the Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 5:1).
he sold the tzemed. The yoke tied on the necks of the cattle.

one who sells the yoke has sold the cow... one who sells the cart has sold the cattle. The commentators found it difficult why one who sells the yoke has sold the cow, whereas in the previous halacha one who sells the tzemed did not sell the cattle. Likewise, why one who sells the cart has sold the cattle, whereas in the previous halacha one who sells the wagon did not sell the mules. Some explained that the distinction stems from ordinary people's speech as customary in their time (Kesef Mishneh and Mirkevet HaMishneh).

and the price is not proof in all these matters and similar ones. The amount of payment is not proof of what the seller meant, and even if the buyer paid the seller a large sum, this is no proof that he sold him anything beyond what he said (see below, halacha 5).
he sold the mardaat. A kind of rug under the saddle.
even though they are not on it. Because a donkey is used for riding, and is not fit for that without these items.
but he did not sell the sack. Which is made for carrying loads and not for riding.
nor the women's carriage. A saddle made for women to ride, as they do not ride in the usual manner of riding.

for if he erred by an amount that the mind inclines to. If the difference between the price paid and the going price is a reasonable difference, such that one could err and think this is the true price.
he has the right to ona'ah or to cancel the sale. In an error of a sixth, the seller returns the difference to him, and in an error of more than a sixth the sale is void (as above 12:2-4).

and if he erred by an amount that the mind does not incline to, the sale is not void, for this is a gift he gave him. If he paid an especially high sum, such that everyone knows it is not the price of a donkey, it is to be assumed that he did so intentionally in order to give the seller a gift.
he sold the clothes on it. The garments it is wearing.
he did not sell the bracelets or the nose rings etc.. Kinds of jewelry.
he sold the siyach. A young donkey.

for no one buys a donkey for its milk. Its milk is good for nothing, and surely the seller did not say 'a nursing donkey' because of the milk, but it is to be assumed that he said so because he meant to transfer the offspring as well (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 5:3).
a limb on which life depends. One cannot live without it.
they assess among themselves. From the word 'shumah': they estimate how much this limb is worth for work.
he did not sell the legs. The front ones, which are important and not secondary to the head.
if he sold the windpipe, he did not sell the liver. Although sometimes they are attached to each other.
but with small livestock etc.. Because it is small and its limbs are worth less, the sale of an important limb includes an unimportant limb.
he sold an ash pit. A pit or container made for refuse.
let it not depart from your eyes. Let it not leave your memory (based on Proverbs 3:21).
for everyone calls it exclusively, without partnership. For all the inhabitants of the place call this thing by this name alone.
as we have explained. Above 26:7-8.
'I am selling you a beit kor of earth'. An area fit for sowing a kor of grain (a kor is a unit of volume equal to thirty se'ah, about two hundred liters), and its area is 75,000 square cubits.
small ravines. Cracks and fissures.
are not measured as part of the beit kor. And he must give him an area of a beit kor apart from those ravines and rocks.
and it appears to him as two or three places. Because of the differences in height between the field and the ravines and rocks.
in what case is this said. That ravines and rocks of less than ten handbreadths are measured with it.
when they were only the area of four kavs. When all the ravines and rocks together take up an area fit for sowing four kavs (two thirds of a se'ah, nearly five liters).
and the four kavs are swallowed up within five kavs. That together with the earth mixed in with them they take up an area of up to five kavs.
and swallowed up within the majority of the field. Those five kavs are swallowed up within an area no larger than a majority of the beit kor (Meiri, Bava Batra 103a).
but if they were more than the area of four kavs... they are not measured with it. For when they are many or scattered it is difficult to plow the field, and the buyer does not waive them.
most of them in a minority of it. Most of the ravines and rocks in a minority of the field.
a minority of them in a majority of it. A minority of the ravines and rocks in the majority of the field.
or they were spread out like a straight thread etc.. The rocks were arranged in a continuous straight line.
at the sides. Like the shape of a star, in which rays emerge in every direction from a central point (R. Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 103a).
a winding line. A twisting line.
all of these are in doubt. In all these cases the rocks are continuous in various shapes, and the doubt is whether they are considered scattered or gathered (see there).

and one who seeks to extract from his fellow bears the burden of proof. If the buyer gave money, he measures those places as part of the field, and if he has not yet given money, the seller need not accept them.

if there was a single rock in it, even the area of a rova of a kor, it is not measured with it. If there is a rock that has a name and importance of its own, it is not nullified relative to the field even if its area is a quarter-kav (Tosafot and other Rishonim, Bava Batra 103b).
and if it was next to the boundary, even the slightest amount, it is not measured with it. A rock adjacent to the boundary of the field is not measured with the field, even if it is very small.
if earth intervened between the rock and the boundary, this is in doubt. There is doubt whether the rock is considered adjacent to the boundary or not.
a measure by the rope. An exact measure.
if it fell short by even the slightest amount, he deducts it from the price. If he gave him less than a beit kor, he returns to him a little of the payment as the value of the shortfall.
and if it exceeded by even the slightest amount, he returns it to him. If he gave him more than a beit kor, the buyer returns the excess.
which is a rova for every se'ah. A quarter-kav in relation to a se'ah is one part in twenty-four.
it suffices him. The party who gained keeps it and the other waives, and the sale stands.

more than this, he calculates with him for all the quarters, all that fell short or exceeded etc.. When the difference between a beit kor and what was actually given is more than the measure of one in twenty-four, the losing party does not waive at all, and the other party must return the entire difference to him (for a similar halacha see above 18:1).
if the surplus was less than nine kavs. If the excess the buyer received is less than nine kavs, which is not considered a field in its own right (see Hilchot Shecheinim 1:4).
he returns the money to him as of the time of the sale. The buyer pays additionally the value of the excess at the time of the sale.
to strengthen the seller's position. Returning money rather than excess land is for the seller's benefit, since a piece of land of less than nine kavs is of no use by itself.
he adjoins it to his other fields. That piece of land is adjacent and connected to another field of the seller, and he suffers no loss in it.

if the surplus was more than nine kavs etc.. Even when the surplus as a whole is more than nine kavs, land is not given to the seller unless the surplus land contains one twenty-fourth of the area (a beit rova for every se'ah) plus nine kavs. If the surplus does not have this measure, the buyer must return money and may not return land (for the reason see Sma, Choshen Mishpat 218:35).

and he gives it to him as of the time he took it from him. Even if the price of land has changed and become more expensive, he must give him the surplus in proportion to what it was at the time of the sale, and he may not reduce for him the amount of land he returns (see below, halacha 8).

but if it was expensive and became cheap etc.. If in the meantime land became cheaper, the seller receives the value of the land as of the time of sale. And if the buyer wishes to pay him with land, he gives an area according to the current price, since in this too we strengthen his position, not to give him land that involves a loss (as above, halacha 7).
half a kav in a garden. This is the minimum measure for defining a garden (see Hilchot Shecheinim 1:4).
he returns to him only money. If the seller wishes.
if the surplus was half a kav, he returns... money. According to the time of sale.
he sold a field and it became a garden. For example, if a spring emerged in that field.
or a garden and it became a field. The spring dried up.

this is in doubt whether he calculates for him etc.. There is doubt whether the calculation explained in the previous halachot is done according to the minimum measure of a field (nine kavs) or according to the minimum measure of a garden (half a kav).
a measure by the rope, whether less or more. Contradictory expressions.
follow the lesser of the expressions. According to the expression that reduces the buyer's power, since his hand is on the bottom because he is not in possession of the land.

and he has only the law that applies whether less or more. The buyer receives according to this law, that we follow the lesser of the expressions, whether he received less than a beit kor (in which case he gets no refund, since the seller told him 'whether less or more') or he received more than a beit kor (in which case he must return, since the seller told him 'a measure by the rope').
and he told him its markers and its boundaries. He defined for him the markers and boundaries of the land.
it fell short by a sixth. If it is found that the size of the land, a beit kor, fell short by a sixth.

it suffices him. The losing party waives. For since he sold him a specific, defined area, although the difference is much greater than one twenty-fourth (the measure for the sale when he says 'beit kor', above, halacha 6), the sale stands as agreed.
it fell short by more than a sixth etc.. If the difference is more than a sixth, there is no waiver, since he stated a specific measure of area.
if what remained in the field etc.. As above, halacha 7.
a field that the buyer knows. He is familiar with it.
it has in its measurement. In its measure.
that is, that it is as good as etc.. The seller meant to say that this field is worth as much as a field whose measure is two hundred.
a letech. Half a beit kor.
as we have explained. Above 26:7-8, 27:11.

three whose purchase is not a purchase and whose sale is not a sale. There is no significance to a purchase or sale that they carry out (and regarding their ability to acquire something given to them as a gift, see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:7).
for the sake of his sustenance. For his livelihood (see below, halacha 6).

or who speaks and does not hear anything. Although for other purposes one who speaks but does not hear is considered of sound mind (see Hilchot Ishut 2:26), with regard to selling land his law is that of a deaf person, since selling land requires sharpness and expertise in business dealings, and since he cannot hear he is not sharp and cannot sell land (Netivot HaMishpat 235:20, Igrot Moshe, Even HaEzer 3:33).
sells and buys by hinting. For a similar law regarding the marriage of a deaf person see Hilchot Gerushin 2:17.
and they settle the matter. They decide with a settled mind.
one who became mute. Lost the ability to speak.

and he is to be examined in the way that one examines for divorce documents. They ask him three questions with pauses in between, and check carefully whether he knows how to answer correctly by nodding his head, to make sure that his mind is settled (Hilchot Gerushin 2:16).
the imbecile. For his definition see Hilchot Edut 9:9.
a guardian is appointed for imbeciles. They appoint a person to oversee the imbecile's property and take care of his needs.
in the way that they appoint one for minors. See Hilchot Nachalot 10:4-5.
at times imbecile and at times sane. Sometimes an imbecile and sometimes clear of mind.
epileptics. Those who suffer from epilepsy.
as we have explained. Above, halacha 1.
as we have explained. Above 12:2-4.

when he took possession by pulling, or caused it to be pulled. He pulled the merchandise when he is the buyer, or gave the buyer the chance to pull when he is the seller (and see above 9:3, that if the minor has not yet received the payment he may retract).

if he gave money for the merchandise and retracted, he does not receive the 'mi shepara' curse etc.. If the minor retracted from the transaction after he paid and before he pulled, he is exempt from anything; whereas one who sold to a minor or bought from him and retracted from the transaction between payment and pulling receives the 'mi shepara' curse (as above 7:1-2).
if they acquired from the hand of the minor. Through kinyan sudar, in which the minor lifted a vessel in order to transfer something belonging to him to another person (see above 5:5).
or he rented the place of the movable goods. He rented the place on which the movables lie, in order to transfer them on that place (see above 3:7).

for nothing is taken from the hand of a minor by law. Money cannot be extracted from a minor by suing him in court, and since in these kinyanim (unlike the kinyanim of pulling and lifting) the merchandise remains in the minor's hand after the act of acquisition, the buyer cannot take it from his hand.

and a kinyan from the hand of a minor is nothing. Other commitments made through kinyan sudar (see above 5:13 in the explanation) likewise do not take effect for a minor (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 26:10).

for a kinyan is like a deed, and the witnesses sign only on the deed of an adult. Kinyan sudar is similar in essence to acquisition by deed, in that in both the acquisition is not accomplished by bringing the object into the buyer's domain (as in kinyan of lifting or pulling) but only through the seller's firm resolve; therefore when the Sages enacted that a minor can sell and buy, they did not enact acquisition for a minor in this manner, which requires greater maturity (based on Birkat Shmuel, Kiddushin, section 26).
and they acquired from their hands. The seller lifted a vessel belonging to the minor in order to transfer the merchandise to the minor.
or he rented from them the place. The minor rented from the seller the place of the movables in order to acquire them.
proof of the matter etc.. Proof that a minor can acquire only when he holds the merchandise in his hand, and not by indirect means.

for a minor's courtyard and his four cubits do not acquire for him. A person's courtyard acquires for him objects that are in it, and likewise when he stands in a public place where few people walk, objects in the four cubits adjacent to him are acquired for him (see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:8-9). This law applies only to an adult, but a minor does not acquire in this way.

because they were included under the law of agency, not under the law of his hand. A courtyard or four cubits acquire for a person by virtue of agency, just as his agent acquires for him, and not because they are considered his hand. Since a minor cannot appoint an agent, he does not acquire by kinyan of courtyard or four cubits (ibid., halacha 10).

as will be explained. Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:8-9 (and Me'iras Einayim wrote that it seems one should emend the Rambam to read 'as was explained', that is, above in Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:10, where this law is explained well with its reason).

but a minor girl whose courtyard was included along with her hand etc.. Regarding a minor girl there is a special teaching: just as she is divorced by a get that reaches her hand, so she is divorced by a get that reaches her courtyard (Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah, ibid.). And just as she acquires a get by kinyan of courtyard, so she acquires merchandise by renting a place and by kinyan sudar.

who bought land, gave the money and took possession. He bought land by paying money and also by using it and performing an act of chazakah (see above 1:8; and see Even HaAzel on why both kinyanim are needed together).
although his sale of land is nothing. Although a minor cannot sell land at all, nevertheless he can acquire in the manner explained here.
for the minor is as if he is not before us. His act is not counted.

and one may act to the benefit of a person in his absence. For the seller acquires on behalf of the minor (Meiri, Bava Batra 155b; and although generally the seller cannot acquire on behalf of the buyer, but the buyer must acquire himself or through another, here the buyer is present and able to acquire but lacks sufficient understanding, and therefore the seller's intent is effective to acquire the land for him - Ketzot HaChoshen, Choshen Mishpat 235:4).

one may act to the benefit of a person in his absence, but may act to his detriment only in his presence. Therefore if the minor wishes he may retract from the transaction (Sma there 235:29, Netivot HaMishpat there 235:18).
and the male has brought two hairs etc.. In the pubic area, which are the signs of adulthood of the male and the female (Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 2:10).
but in land their acts are not valid. Because a land transaction requires special expertise, and the Sages feared he would lose his money (Aruch HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 235:13).
lest he sell cheaply because his mind inclines toward the money. There is concern that he does not sufficiently appreciate the land, since he did not toil over it or pay for it.
the gift of one who is gravely ill. Who gave a gift while ill.
it stands. Even land he received by inheritance that he cannot sell, he can give as a gift.
for had he not received great benefit, he would not have given. A person usually gives a gift only when he owes a favor to the giver or expects to receive a favor from him.

and it is something that is not common. Another reason the Sages annulled only the sale and not the gift is that a gift of land is not so common, and the Sages did not worry about making an enactment about something uncommon.

and the Sages said his gift shall stand so that his words will be heeded. A third reason is that the ability to give a gift benefits him socially, so that people will listen to him and wish to help him.

or when signs of saris have developed in him. Signs indicating a defect in his sexual development (for details see Hilchot Ishut 2:13), and therefore when he reaches the age of twenty minus thirty days he is considered an adult even though he did not bring two hairs (see ibid., halacha 11).
even in his own property. Even property of his that he did not inherit, he cannot sell.
until he reaches the majority of his years. Age thirty-five and one day (ibid.).
and they sought to examine him. After he was buried.
we do not listen to them, so as not to disgrace him. Out of respect for the dead.
for the signs are liable to change at death. And it is possible that he had signs before he died.
whether before twenty or after twenty. For if he sold the land before the age of twenty he can take it back from the buyer even if he is now past twenty.
and he recovers from the buyer all the produce he ate. The buyer must pay him for what he ate, since the sale was not valid.
and if he incurred expenses. If the buyer spent his own money for the land.
they assess for him and he returns the rest. They assess how much of the produce he ate covers his expenses, and he pays for the remaining produce.

it is established in the buyer's hand, for he was content with his sale. The sale became final, since the seller revealed his consent to it after reaching the age of twenty, and he is like one who sold his father's property after the age of twenty.
and he acquired it for the buyer without his knowledge. Through another person who performed a kinyan on behalf of the buyer.
the buyer's hand is on top. For a similar halacha regarding a gift see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:2.
a deed is written for the seller even though the buyer is not with him. For the buyer can still refuse the sale (see also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 24:1).

and always the buyer pays the scribe's fee, even if he sold his field because of its poor quality. In every sale the buyer pays the scribe who writes the deed, for even in a sale made because the field is poor, the buyer's benefit is greater than the seller's. In addition, the buyer is the one who needs the deed as proof of his ownership (R. Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 167b).
and he does not need to acquire anything from him. There is no need to perform a kinyan sudar to strengthen the master's words (see above 5:13); his statement that he confirms or cancels suffices.
the slave. A Canaanite slave.
the master's hand is on top. Because a slave has no property of his own (see Hilchot Sheelah UFikadon 3:2).

in the tzon barzel property she brought him. Property that the wife brought with her at the time of marriage, and the husband took on responsibility to restore its value in case of divorce or widowhood (Hilchot Ishut 16:1).
in the things that he designated for her in her ketubah. Property designated for collection of the ketubah.

in melog property. Property that the wife brought with her at the time of marriage, from which the husband benefits but the principal of the property is not his and he does not take responsibility for it (ibid.).

if he wished to uphold. The act that the wife performed with her husband's property stands if the husband approves it, since the wife's hand is like her husband's hand, and when he agrees to it her act is considered his act. Likewise regarding tzon barzel and melog property, in which the agreement of both is needed, the wife revealed her consent at the time of the act, and when the husband agrees to it, it turns out that both agreed.

if he wished to cancel everything. However, in melog property he may not remove the principal of the property from the buyer's hand but only the produce, and if the wife dies during her husband's lifetime, he may remove the principal as well from the buyer (ibid. 22:7).
land that his wife brought him in her ketubah. Land that she brought with her and which was recorded in the ketubah.

land that he brought in for her, valued, from his own. Land that the husband gave the wife against the valuation of the dowry she brought from her father's house, as an addition to the dowry (see Hilchot Ishut 23:11).

everything he did is void, because she says, 'I did it to please my husband'. The wife can claim that she upheld her husband's act in order to appease him but did not agree to it wholeheartedly (see also ibid. 22:15; and all this is in tzon barzel property, but in melog property she cannot make this claim, as explained in the next halacha).

if she wished to cancel, she may cancel; and if she upheld his acts, the buyers acquired. For the sale of melog property takes effect only with the agreement of both, and she cannot claim that she agreed only to please her husband, because melog property is entirely hers and she is not afraid to protest when he sells it (see also Hilchot Ishut 22:16-17).
although he is not permitted. For the principal of the property is hers.

the buyers acquired. Because a wife does not rely on movables as financial security as she relies on land, since land remains forever whereas movables may perish, and it makes no difference to her whether they perish or the husband sells them, since either way he owes her their value in case of divorce or widowhood (Maggid Mishneh, and see also Hilchot Ishut 22:16).
even though they are under the lien of the ketubah. Although all his property is liable for her ketubah (Hilchot Ishut 16:10).
and if she comes to collect, she collects. If she is divorced or widowed and there is no other property from which to collect, she removes the property from the buyer's hand (ibid.).

unless she wrote to the buyer beforehand and they acquired from her hand. Unless she committed herself to the buyer before the sale, in writing and by kinyan sudar, that she would not collect from him (see ibid. 17:11).
he did not acquire, and she may retract and take it out of his hand. For she can claim that she did it to please him and not wholeheartedly.
as we have explained in Hilchot Ishut. 22:18.

their purchase is a purchase and their sale is a sale. For the court or the guardian must look after orphans (Hilchot Nachalot 10:5), and they have authority to carry out a transaction for their benefit (see ibid. 11:6-8, that the authority applies only to a transaction that will certainly benefit the orphans).
even though he is beaten. Disciplinary lashes, for violating the prohibition the Sages decreed against this, lest he come to write (Hilchot Shabbat 23:12).
who made a kinyan from his hand on Shabbat. Who committed himself to something in particular by kinyan sudar.
and they write after Shabbat and give. The witnesses to the kinyan write a document about the content of the kinyan, and give it to the one entitled to it.
